summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the amount of income from the money lending investments. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who agreed with the Tribunal that the judgment of the High Court was binding on it and accordingly rejected the appeal. On further appeal by the Revenue, the High court held that the decision of the Orissa High Court in Vedreva Venkappa Rao vs Commissioner of Wealth Tax (AIR was binding upon it, and accordingly dismissed the appeals. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The principle laid down in Vedresvu Venkappa Reddy 's case is not applicable to a case where there are different previous years under the Income Tax Act for different sources of income. [310F] 2.1 In the instant case, the assessee was liable to be assessed to Wealth tax for assessment years 1966 67, 1967 68 and 1967 69 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965, March 31 and 31, 1967). The expression "net wealth" is defined in cl. (m) of section 2 of the Act as meaning the amount by which the aggregate value of all the assets, wherever located, belonging to the assessee on the valuation date. All the assets of the assessee bar those expressly excepted by the statute, are to be taken into account and it is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of accounting or another. [309G H] 2:2 The assets to be considered are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accounts adopted by the assessee. The assets are not confined to cash. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (1) of s.7 as the estimated price which, in the opinion of the Wealth Tax officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the value date. In other words, it would be the estimated open market value of the rights in the property which constitute the asset. When we speak of the value of a property, on a legal plane, there is an obvious advantage in adopting as the valuation dates the last day of a period which is also the relevant period under the income tax Act.

The respondent was a Sub Inspector of Police. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had not maintained absolute integrity and devotion to duty in as much as he had no t erned by himself to perform his duties. The respondent filed an appeal before the Appellate Authority which was dis missed. The Tribunal set aside the order of dismissal and directed reinstatement with full back wages. The appellant filed a writ petition challenging the findings of the Inquiry Officer that he was the master mind behind the scheme to defrauded the Government servant, and that he should not be allowed to cross examine the witnesses in t he case. The High Court held that the Tribunal had no power to interfere with the penalty on the basis of the enquiry report. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the Appellate Commis sioner had no powers to interfere, and the Tribunal erred in directing re opening the evidence. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Appellate Authority has not interfered with the findings arrived at by the Inquiry Offi cer or the competent authority where the recording of evidence and on consideration of t he scope of jurisdiction and amplitude of power of the Tribunal was vitiated because of the use of inadmissible material for withdrawal of salary in the disciplinary proceedings. [436C] 2. The Tribunals have no such discretion or power. It is only to see whether the punishment imposed by a disciplinary authority is fair and proper in the circumstances of the case. If the penalty can lawfully be imposed and is imposed on the proved misconduct, the Tribunal has no power under article 323A or article 226 of the Constitution to interfere. [35D E] 3. The power to impose penalty on a delinquent officer is conferred on the competent au thority either by an Act of legislature or rules made under the provisions of the Indian Income Tax Act. If there has been an enquiry consistent with the prescribed rules, it is not for the Court to consider whether that ground alone would have weighed with the authority in dismissing the public servant. Where the person without enquiry is found guilty, removed or reduced in rank solely on the su ch basis of conviction by a criminal court, the tribunal may examine the adequacy of the penalty imposed in the light of the provisions and sentence inflicted on the person. If it is found that there was legal evidence to show that the punishment matter minded was not suitable for the Supreme Court or that the authority had no jurisdiction to substitute its own discretion for that of the authority, the order would be quashed. [36E F] 4. The disciplinary authority must, however, bear in mind that the penalty cannot be equated with an appellate jurisdiction. The tribunal cannot interfere with a finding of fact or evidence unless it is perverse. It has no such power or jurisdiction. [37F G] 5. In the instant case, the findings are not perverse and the High Court has no jurisdiction under Article 226 to interfere in exercise of its powers. [38G] 6. The question whether the respondent was guilty of the charge framed against him was a mindful one or not.

The appellant plaintiff filed a suit for eviction of the defendant from the property in question. The suit was dismissed on the ground that he was not in possession of the premises within the meaning of section 2(3) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The Trial Court held that the plaintiff was not entitled to an injunction as prayed for by him. In appeal, the High Court held (i) that the suit was barred by res judicata because the plaintiff had in fact been dispossessed from the premises on or about May 6, 1968; (ii) that he had been forcibly dispossessed from a portion of the property and was therefore liable to be evicted therefrom; and (iii) that it was only thereafter that the appellant could seek possession of that portion of his property. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that since the plaintiff 's tenancy was terminated by efflux of time and he had paid the first instalment of rent for the year 1968, he was in no way entitled to be dispossessed from that portion or any of them claim to be remedy available to him in respect of that cause of action. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the Trial Court was wrong in holding the suit for a mere declaration without seeking consequential relief for possession. [1033C] 2.1 The Act does not preclude the institution of a suit by a tenant for restoration of possession from a trespasser. If the defendant who is sued as a trespasser raises a plea of tenancy, a question arises whether his plea of the tenancy can be decided by the Civil Court as incidental to the grant of relief for posession or is the Civil court precluded from deciding even incidentally. [1133E] 2:2 The Act makes it applicable to pending suits also. However, the Act does provide that if any question arises as to whether any person is a tenant or should be deemed to be a tenant under the Act, the Mamlatdar shall decide such question. [1234F G] 3.1 Section 7 of the Act provides that if in any suit instituted in a Civil Court issues which are required to be settled, decided and dealt with by the Mamlatdar, the Civil Judge may consider passing of a decree in eviction but if on the other hand he is held to be tenant, the civil court may be required to dismiss the suit. If on the one hand hears his claim to bring the suit within the jurisdiction of any Court he will thereafter be precluded from determining or deciding the same in view of section 7 read with section 58(2) of Act. [1534G H] 3:3.

The petitioners are daily rated employees of the respondent Corporation. They were paid minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. The petitioners filed a writ petition in this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the constitutional validity of the provisions of the . It was contended on their behalf that the unit where they were working was a factory registered under the Factories Act and that the establishment was not encouraging, and that it had reduced its overheads and maintained only the administrative staff in the production centers at different parts of the State and no permanent craftsmen were employed. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of "equal pay for equal work" cannot be enforced invariably in every kind of service particularly in the area of professional services. [668 E] 2. The law relating to equal pay for Equal work has been practically hammered out and very little remains for further innovation. In the light of the principles, this court may now consider whether the equality claims of the petitioners could be allowed. [669 F G] Randhir Singh vs Union of India, ; , referred to. 3. The proposition that equal pay cannot be invoked invariably in all kind of services particularly in tho area of profession is not correct. The distinction between physical activity and physical activity is expressly guaranteed by our Constitution. The princi plete has to be read into Article 14 of the constitution which enjoins the State not to deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the law and also to Article 16 which declares that there should be equality of opportunity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. [667 G H] 4. The equality claims are of equal pay. The discrimination complained of must be within the same estab lishment owned by the same management. A comparison cannot be made with counterparts in other establishments with different management, or even in establishments in different geographical proximity though owned by same master. Unless it is shown that there is a discrimination amongst the same set of employees by the very master in the same establishment, the principle of 'equal pay ' cannot be enforce ed. This was also the view expressed in Federation of All India Customs and Central Excise Stenographers (Recognised) vs Union Of India, [1987] 2 S.C.R.

The prosecution case was that on the night of occurrence and on the allegation that in pursuance of a conspiracy to commit murder of one Malan, daughter of Kishan and two others, the deceased daughter of the deceased and his wife, the appellant and three others were committed for committing murders of young girls and women in the vicinity of the victims or disfiguring their faces in order to make it appear that the accused in pursuance thereof committed the murder of Malan. The trial court found the accused guilty under section 302 read with section 120B I.P.C. and acquitted them. On appeal, the High Court set aside his conviction and sentence awarded to him. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the conviction of the accused alone for conspiracy under section302 read with Section 120B IPC could be sustained. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confession of accused 5 could not be relied upon against accused 6 in view of the fact that he had been acquitted by the trial court of charge No. 1 framed under section 307 read with s.120B I P.C., and accused 5 was not charged for the offence of murder of M.P.[778E F] 2. The High Court has rightly considered the evidence and dismissed the appeal filed by the State against acquittal of accused 6 and convicted him under section 201 read with S.120 B I. P. C. [778F G] 3. The evidence of the approver P.W. 1 and the retracted confession of the co accused 5, that is, recovery of the razor blade, article 54, persuant to the confessional statement of accused No. 6, admitted under section 27 Evidence Act, and no appeal against their acquittal had been filed in this Court. [783G H] 4.

The appellant executed a will in favour of the respondent, who was the wife of the testator. The will provided that the testator would execute a power of attorney in respect of certain properties including items 3, 4 and 5 mentioned in the will. The testator died on January 14, 1944. After his death, the appellant filed a suit for possession of the properties covered by the said Will. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the will was not genuine and that it was not proved to be last will and testament of the deceased testator. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The evidence on record shows that the appellant had received a large sum of money from his sons as consideration for the properties conveyed by the will and had received substantial benefit under it. [447 D] (ii) The will was executed in the presence of the two attesting witnesses and there was no suggestion to the effect that the Will was not registered. The evidence showed that the executant had received large sums of money and the husband had received considerable benefit under the will, that is, the amount of the property covered by it. The appellant had also failed to prove that the testatrix fully understood the nature and effect of its contents. [458 E] (iii) The High Court was in error in coming to the conclusion that it could not be said that the execution of the will had been proved by the attesting witnesses. [459 G] (iv) The finding of the High court on the question of the due execution of a will is justified and must be upheld. [465 B C] (v) The testator 's evidence was very clear and definite in regard to the execution and disposition of the Will. It was not shown that the propounder had any clear recollection as to what happened on the day when he attested the will or that there was any suspicious circumstances surrounding the execution thereof. [467 G] In the present case, the High Courts were justified in coming into the conclusion, that it is not shown by the appellant that the attesting witness was misled or misled by his signature. The Will was executed by the testator on the same day and it was at his dictation that the scribe wrote the will to the scribe. [468 A] (vi) The question whether the propounder has been able to prove the transfer of the title or its extinction by adverse possession respectively depends upon the circumstances of each case. If the propounder is a party writes or prepares a will under which he takes advantage, that itself is generally treated as a suspicious circumstance attending the execution. [470 B] (vii) The onus was on the propounder to prove his transfer of title or their extinction by cogent and satisfactory evidence. [471 C] In re: G.I.R. , referred to. (viii) The burden of proving that the instrument was produced before the court is on the plaintiff. It is not necessary for the propounder, in a case where the onus is on him to prove affirmatively that the document was not his will or not.

The appellant company was carrying on business of manufacturing Arcotors, known as "Cinema Arc Carbons" and was doing the business of selling Arcottons. The goods were sold by the appellant to its dealers who were running cinemas or for any other use. The sales tax authorities held that they fell under entry No. 4 of the first schedule of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957, and that they fall under Entry No. 5 of Schedule 1 of the Act. This view was upheld by the Andhra pradesh High Court in the State of Andhra Pradesh vs Srimathi Nidmarthi Saraswathi Devi, ; , holding that the common or ordinary use of the are carbons was that they exuded their power foul light cast through the projectors on cinema screens and that the sales tax Appellate Tribunal, the final departmental authority under the Act had allowed an application for adducing expert evidence to determine the question whether these were carbins manufactured by the appellants. The High Court held that the main use of these are carbolicies was that the exuded electric light used in projectors in cinemas and not that of a motor vehicle. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The word "accessories" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word accessory is used is given in Webster 's Third New International Dictionary as follows: "all objects or device that is not essential in itself but that adds to the beauty, convenience, or effectiveness of something else". [562 E] (2) The definition of "accessory" is not exhaustive in which it is an accessory. It is not enough to show that the article can be put to other uses also. It was its general or predominant user which seems to determine its category in which an article will fall. The first entry in the Schedule relates to "motor vehicles". The words "parts thereof" are used in several entries, such as entry No 6 for clocks, time pieces and watches, entry No 11 for dictaphones and other similar apparatus for recording sound, and entry No 12 for dictating, stage lighting, or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required. [562 F] (3) The words 'parts thereto ' are used to denote a connection with electricity, nor their utilisation in a process involving application of electrical power could convert them into "electrical goods" as contemplated by Entry No 4. Consequently, the goods under consideration are covered by the relevant entry No 4 of Schedule I of the Madras General Sales tax Act, and the appellant is entitled to claim exemption from tax for two assessment years 1965 66 and 1966 77 on the ground that they fail under Entry 4 of schedule 1 of Andhra Act. [563 G 564 A] (4) The fact that they can also be used for search lights, signalling, stage burning, or when powerful lighting is required cannot detract from the classification to which the carbon ares belong. That is determined by their ordinary or commonly known purpose or user. This, as already observed, is evident from the fact that the term "accessors" is use in the schedules to describe the goods which might have been manu factured for use. [564 B C] (5) The expression "part of motor vehicles" is given a sense in the Act in a schedule in which descriptions of goods to be taxed indicate that the expression "required for use there with" has been employed for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. For instance, in entry No 5 of schedule I of Andhra pra burnt equipment, the description so given so.

The petitioners in these petitions challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government under section 15 of the (67 of 1957) amending the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966, with retrospective effect from 1 7 1985 and substituting the original rule 21 for the former Rule 21. The High Court dismissed their writ petitions holding that the impugned notification was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. In these appeals by special leave it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the royalty levied and covered under the Rules should be applied only for mineral development and since the said royalty was being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State, the levy was bad; and that the notification in question was in violation of clause(b) and was therefore invalid. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The levy is made under a law made by the Central Government for purposes of regulation and development and conservation of minerals. It is equally clear that while levying a tax the authority is entitled to grant concessions and exemptions wherever necessary having regard to the purpose of the Act, the imposition of royalty is incidental to the regulation and Development of minerals [412C D] 2. The expression "minerals" in clause (a) of article 304 has no relevance on the point in question. No restriction is being imposed on the freedom of trade of the Petitioners by the levy of royalty. The minerals belong to the Government and if anybody wants to have the right as a lessee to exploit the mines in question to the exclusion of all others and to remove the minerals with a view to making profit, he has to pay a royalty imposed in accordance with law. [415D E] 3. The Act under the rules was made for purposes other than the former rule 21 was invalid as it was discriminatory in character. It was not an imposition made by a law making the rules equi putely with a welfare State. [414E F] 4.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliars of Manjakollai village in the District of Nagapattinam. The appellant challenged the election on the ground that the trusteeship of the Kumaran Koil was not hereditary and that the suit was not barred by limitation. The High Court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge and restored that of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the succession is "regulated by usage" and the words "succession to this office" in section 6(9) of the Madras Act 19 of 1951 must be construed along with the phrase "suecession to the office" and when so construed, part of the definition would only apply where the ordinary rules of succession under the Hindu law are modified by usage and succession has to be determined in accordance with the modified rules. HELD: (i) The word "sucession" in relation to property and rights and interests in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another". In the case of mutts, whose heads are often celibates and sometimes sanyasins, special rules of inheritance obtain by custom and usage. In Sital Das vs Sant Ram (I.L.R. , approved. (ii) The phrase "regulatedby usage" in Section 6(1)(9) must be interpreted along with 'the phrase " succession" and not as "supendents" in the sense that on the expiry of the term of succession, the office of a hereditary trustee is in the nature of property. This is so whether the trustee has a beneficial interest of some sort or not.

The prosecution case against the appellant was that he along with others, armed with a knife and other weapons went to the scene of occurrence and attacked the deceased with knife. The deceased succumbed to his injuries on the spot. The trial court acquitted the second accused. On appeal by special leave, the High Court acquitted the first accused. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the testimony of PW 4 in so far as he implicated the second appellant is inconsistent with the evidence given out by the prosecution witnesses and described him as an absconder. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court has not considered the intrinsic quality of the evidence of PW4. It failed to notice certain broad facts which should definitely weigh with the court while appreciating ocular testimony. From the medical evidence it is clear that there were more than one assailant and yet for the FIR it appears that there was only one assailant. This may not, in a given case, be considered as a very serious infirmity since the witness may not have seen the other. assailants when he came running to the place of occurrence. But the fact that the witness has stated in the first information report that the deceased was only mentioning the name of accused workman, this earlier version appears to be contradicted by the medical evi dence. [711E F] 2. The very fact that this eye witness could be persuaded to substitute PWs 1, 2 and 3 for his deceased brother as chasing the assailants, degrades him from the status of an absolutely reliable witness. He is definitely an obliging witness and cannot at all be trustworthy. This witness may also not have a quali ficable or truthful version in implicating the accused for the mere asking by someone, if not by the inimical police officer (PW 23) against whom criminal cases were pending at the instance of the accused 's father. Apart from that there is no evidence to show that the witnesses who gathered would not ask PW 4, who arrived at the place a little later than PW 4. [612F H] 3. The mere fact that PW 4 stated in his first information Report that the appellant had assaulted him with knife cannot be taken into consideration as a mere irregularity. It is difficult to accept this explanation of the witness because he has deliberately changed his own stand in court when he deposed that he saw two other persons running ahead of accused and his father on the one hand and the deceased chasing him from behind. [1112F G] 4. The first version could not be accepted as a most serious infirmity because the witness might not have heard the other assailants when they came running towards the place where he fell dead. On the other hand it is conceivable that those persons who arrived on hearing the shout of his deceased were trying to lose his life in such a serious charge.

The assessee firm was carrying on business in the years 1950 51 and 1951 52. The partnership was carried on by one Amarchand and Hiralal as their partners. The firm kept its accounts on cash basis. For the assessment year 1950 51 the Income tax Officer sought to tax these realisations. The assessments were made for the assessment years 195051 and 195152 but the assessments were quashed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Commissioner of Income tax took an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal which held that the notices under section 34 could validly be served only for the year 1950 52 and notices for subsequent years were invalid. The High Court, on reference, answered the question in the negative and against the assessee. Held, that the amounts received by the heirs and legal representatives of Amarchand were not liable to tax as they were not income which may be deemed to have been received by them under the provisions of section 24B of the Income Tax Act. The provisions of s.24B do not extend to tax liability of the estate of a deceased person beyond the previous or the account year in which that person dies. The provision of section 23(1) does not extend the liability of estate of the deceased person upto the date of his death and the income received by him before his death is not liable for payment of income tax in the several years of assessment. Ellis C. Reid vs Commissioner of Incometax, Bombay, , applied. The amounts which were sought to be taxed and which have been held not to be liable to income tax are those which were not received in the previous year and are therefore not liable under section 24 B.

The petitioners were appointed between December 27, 1956 and July 4, 1968. They challenged the provisions of the , as ultra vires the Constitution on the ground that article 16(3) under which they and their agents were appointed after March 21, 1959, was violated by the provision for appointment to posts in the Secretariat Departments and that the said provision was arbitrary and violative of Article 16(1). The High Court dismissed the petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that article 3(3), under which the Act and the Rules purport to be made, had been misunderstood as conferring a power to make a law prescribing conditions as to residence in a part of a State. HELD : (i) The words "any requirement" cannot be read to warrant something which could have been said more specifically. These words bear upon the kind of residence or its duration rather than its location within the State. [121 E] (ii) Article 35(a) does not require that the narrow construction upon the exception should be placed as indeed the debates in the Constituent Assembly also seem to indicate. The word "State" is used in the widest sense in so far as the Constitution makes it clear that a whole State as the venue for residential qualification and it is impossible to think that the Constituent Committee was thinking of residence in Districts, Taluqas, cities, towns etc. more appropriate and specific language could have be used such as 'any requirement as to the residence within that State or Union territory prior to employment or appointment to an office in that State 'or Union territory. [122 E F] (iii) The word 'State ' in section 3 of the Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act, 1957, is not read to mean "any requirements as to residential within the state or Union Territory prior to appointment" and any requirement may be prescribed by rules made under article 372.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr Post Office. He was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Offices Act, 1898 and in two of them also for offences of theft and forgery. The trial court acquitted him but on appeal the High Court held that the appellant had secreted the five registered letters in question and on this finding set aside his acquittal and convicted him under section 51 of the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the prosecution having merely shown that the registered letters were recovered from the possession of the appellant, the mere fact that there was even a delay of several months in delivering a postal article to the addressee would not mean that the article had ceased to be in course of transmission by post. HELD : The mere fact of possession does not suffice to show that the articles were secreted by the appellant. [415 D] (i) In a case like this where the entrustment of an article is made an ingredient of an offence, the legislature has used appropriate words to make the matter clear. If there was no such thing as to the contents of the letters in the post office, then it would have used language similar to that used by it in section 55. It is common experience that delivery of postal articles is the sine qua non for its transmission. [414 E F] (ii) The mere circumstance that there is even a delayed delivery does not necessarily render the article incomplete. [416 G] (iii) In the present case, the appellant was given notice under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and he had been convicted under section 53 without giving any notice to him. Therefore, the conviction could not be sustained.

The appellant, a public servant, filed a complaint before the Nyaya Panchayat alleging that he had been abused and assaulted by the complainant. The Magistrate passed an order staying proceedings pending before him. The appellant 's application under section 85 of the U.P. Panchayat Raj Act, 1947 was dismissed by the District Magistrate on the ground that the complainant did not give the date of the High Court 's stay order. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Courts had not given any reasons for holding that the appellant stayed proceedings before the 226 Nyaya Panchayat and that the matter should be remanded to the Nyaya Panchayats for a proper enquiry. HELD : The High Court was wrong in interfering with the orders of the District Magistrates. [119D] (a) The High Courts were not justified in interfering under section 4 and 5 of the Act. The High court did not appreciate that the so called affidavit which was filed before the District Magis trate was in fact not an affidavit at all. It had not been sworn to before any person authorised to administer oaths. [120E] (b) In such matters those who assert that a person had knowledge of the order must prove this fact beyond all reasonable doubt. If there is any doubt, the benefit ought to be given to the person charged with contempt of court. If a person bona fide comes to the conclusion on the material placed before him that the source of information is not authentic he cannot be held guilty of contempt of Court for disobeying its order unless there is unimpeachable evidence that the judicial officer had knowledge or had knowledge about the order of the high Court. [121H; 122A] (c) The appellant was not a party authorised to administering oaths and, therefore, the High court should not have drawn an adverse inference from the fact that the reasons for not accepting the prayer for stay were not recorded. [122B C] (d) The order of a District Magistrate was passed in a complaint filed by the appellant against the respondents. The order did not contain the date or the order even a copy of the telegram was not attached to the application; and the application was made after the proceedings on that date had commenced and evidence taken.

The appellant was tried and convicted for the murder of Sheo Sahai. The Sessions Judge accepted his version and convicted him under section 302, I.P.C., but acquitted him on the ground that he had no motive to kill Sheo Sahai and that he was falsely implicated in the case. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the conviction of the appellant under section 307, I P.C. must be set aside and his conviction under section 201, I .P. C., must be upheld. The evidence against the appellant was circumstantial and not a chain of evidence. The murder was committed in the month of June, 1960 between the two on account of the temperature and on account oth er of the culprit 's desire to wash of blood marks on his person, the appellant 's bathing in the Canal at that hour of the night cannot be said to have been improbable. The appellant had been rightly convicted of the offence under section 364 I. P. C. He was rightly convicted for murder and sentenced to death. The circumstantial evidence established against him fully establish that the appellant had a motive to harm Sheo Sahai, and that the deceased had purchased a sword a day before the incident and deposited it with the police station after he had dictated the report. The extra judicial confession of the accused to the effect that he did purchase a sword was not admissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a direct admission of the guilt of the appel lant. The conviction of appellant under s.302, IP.c., must therefore be setaside and his sentence of death passed on him must be reduced to one of life imprisonment.

The Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 was enacted by the State Legislature to issue a notification for holding election to the Municipality. The Collector issued a public notice under Rule 4(1) of the Rules calling upon persons whose names had not been included in the electoral roll and who claimed to be included in that list. The final publication of the electoral rolls under Rule 8 of the rules was done on November 16, 1978 notifying that the poll would take place on December 31, 1978 in all the 44 constituencies: and that claims or objections which had not yet been preferred as required under the Rules should be rejected. The respondent No. 1 filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the election to fill up the vacancies and for declaration of the result thereof. The High Court allowed the petition holding that respondent No 2 was not entitled to any relief under Article 226 of the Constitution on account of inordinate delay involved in the presentation of the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The power of the High Courts under article 226 of The Constitution to issue an appropriate writ is discretionary and if the High court finds that there is not satisfactory explanation for the delay in filing the petition, such a step may reject the petition if it finds that the issue of Writ will lead to public inconvenience and interference with rights of others. This rule applies also to a case where the validity or claim cannot be preferred to the petitioner under Article 32. [497C D] 1.2 The power to issue writ is discretion and if High Court finds that no such claim or objection has been preferred, it may reject an application for the purpose of hearing. No such appeal was presented. The order of the Single Judge was set aside by the Division Bench on the ground that it was only on December S, 1978 for the first time that the attention of the Collector was drawn to the error that had crept into the notice published under Rule 1 of the Madhya Pradesh Rules. By that time the nominations had all been received. The finality of the decision with regard to the election should be given effect to. [498D E] 2.1 In the instant case, the writ petitioners were not entitled as they had approached the Court after undue delay.

The appellant was the director of a company and its directors were prosecuted under section 32(5) of the , for failure to comply with the provisions of section 220(1) of that Act. The High Court held that if no balance sheet is laid before a general body meeting, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 132 and that the appellant was guilty of an offence under section 134(4). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the principle accepted by this Court in Park vs Lawton, , that a company or its directors in a prosecution under section 12 of the 1913 Act could not rely upon their failure to call the general body meetings and to lay the balance sheet and profit and loss account before it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act; (2) the provision in section 134 was ultra vires article 19(1)(c) of Constitution because, (a) the holding of the annual general meeting and the laying before it of the balance sheets and profit & loss account were laid before the general meeting; (b) the failure to do so did not make him liable under the provisions Of section 134 (4); and (c) the appellant had failed to call a general meeting as required by section 134. HELD : (i) The High Courts have taken a similar view in respect of Park vs lawton, ; , that the holding was not an offence within the meaning of section 134 of the 1956 Act or section 220 of the Indian Penal Code. [415 D] (ii) The appellant could not be convicted under section 135(5). A different offence might have been committed either under section 76(2) or under section 133(3). It is possible to conceive of the law providing that the balance Sheet and profit or loss account shall be sent to the Registrar even without the necessity of their being laid before him. The intention was made further clear by the provision under sub section (2), namely, that if the balancesheet is not adopted at the general meetings before which it is laid, a statement of that fact and of the reasons therefore have to be annexed to the balance Sheets and profit, account or the income and expenditure account, as the case may be, would be made punishable under sub s.(4) of section 135. [416 G H] (iii) The penalty under section 132 is for default in complying with those provisions. A different punishment might have already been committed by the directors in contravention of section 12 but not under section 13. [414 C D] In re Kavalappara Pillai, , referred to. (iv) The State vs Linkers Private Ltd., ; , followed.

The West Bengal Special Courts Act of 1950, which was enacted to provide for the speedier trial of certain offences and sections 3 and 4 of the Act provided that a special court shall try such offences or classes of cases as it thinks fit. The appellant who was one of the accused in the case filed a complaint against him under section 3 Of the West Bengal Criminal Courts Act, 1950, alleging that he had committed offences punishable by offences under sections 3, 4 and 6 of the said Act. He contended that the Act did not provide for speediers trial but only provided for trials to be tried by Special Court constituted under the Act and that the State Government was incompetent to try such cases as were made the subject matter of the special procedure laid down in the Code of Criminal Procedure. Held, that the provisions of section 5(1) Of the Act which authorises the State government to direct a case to be committed by a Special Court for trial by a special Court, do not contravene article 14 and are therefore void. The scheme of the impugned Act is that the Special Court shall try all offences or cases or classes or cases of cases or cases, or classes thereof, as the State Govern ment may by general or special order in writing direct. It does not make any difference whether a case or class of cases is covered by the provisions contained in section 5 (1) of the WestBengal Special Courts (Special Courts) Act, 1951, and the latter Act offends against article 14 of the Constitution. The classification implied in this part of the sub section has no application to such cases. It is not necessary that the Legislature should be a proper classification so as not to offend against the Constitution but only for the purpose of showing exactly the offences which in its opinion are likely to be likely to produce some inequality and thereby affect the community at large. The fact that it gives unrelareable power to the State Govt. to make a classification of offences, classes of offences or class or cases does not mean that judges are to deter mine what is for the good of the people and substitute their individual and personal opinions for that of the government of the day, or that they may usurp the functions of the legislature.

The appellant, a Professor in the Medical College of Delhi, was appointed as Associate Professor of Radiology in the Institute of Radiotherapy. The post of Associate Professor in that Institute was attached to the Maulana Azad Medical College, New Delhi. The appellant was selected by the Selection Committee constituted for selection to the Specialists ' Grade with effect from January 14, 1963. On August 19, 1966, the appellant was appointed to the said post on a regular basis till October 8, 1964. In the letter of appointment he was shown as an Associate Professor and was confirmed in the post of Assistant Professor in a Medical College. The respondent No. 1, who was working as a Reader in the Hospital, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of his appointment on the ground that he had been appointed to that post by direct recruitment through the UPSC at the level of lecturer in the Government College and therefore he did not possess the requisite teaching experience under the Central Health Service. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant possessed the necessary qualifications for being appointed as Professor of radiology in Malulana Azad medical college, NewDelhi. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the post was a teaching post and not an Assistant Professor or Professor of Pathology; (ii) the appellant having been appointed by direct recruit through the Commission of Inquiry, he was not holding the post as an Assistant Director of Radiologist in the Health Department; (iii) the appointment of the respondent No 1 to the post on selection to that category was illegal and violative of articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution; and (iv) the High Courts were wrong in holding that he was entitled to seniority over and above the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The word 'as ' in the collocation of words used in paragraph 3 of Annexure I to the Second Schedule to the Rules means "in the capacity of". [8E] (2) The post is a teaching posts and does not make it an establishment post. It was a post belonging to specialist Grade II which is equivalent to Supertime grade II carrying a pay scale of Rs. 200/ per month. The fact that the post is not a teaching Post does not give him a right to hold the post. [8F G] (3) The appellant could not be considered to have held the post for selection as he was holding the posts of Associate Professors in the University Medical College or teaching institution with the ex officio designation. [9H; 10A B] (4) The appointment of respondent No, 1 to this post is made by promotion through UPSC at a time when the rules came into force and it is not necessary that the teaching experience gained by him while holding a non teaching post in a teaching hospital like the appellant could be taken into consideration. [10E F] (5) The fact of the post being a selection of Assistant Professors, there was no provision for appointment to the posts in the Post Graduate Medical Colleges and teaching institutions. [11F G]. (6) The respondent had not acquired the status of an Associate professor of Radiological Teaching as he did. not have any teaching experience as such. [12A B]. (7) The High Courts should not have interfered with the order made by the Government of India, Ministry of Health and Family Planning, Department of Health in holding on a misconstruction of r. 8(2) that the word ' as ' in para 3 of the Annexure I of the Second schedule must be interpreted to mean "initially teaching post". [12E F].

The appellant company had entered into a contract with the respondent company for the production of paper on a very large scale. The workmen were paid minimum wages at the time of the agreement and there was no dispute about this payment. The Company did not fix the minimum wage in accordance with the minimum wages being paid in those industries. The Tribunal found that there were no other concerns in the same region in which the company was working, that the workmen were really paying much lower wages than the minimum, that they had been paid more than what was paid to the lowest paid worker in some of the Paper Mills outside the region and that the Company was paying profit bonus equivalent to three months ' basic wage. The High Court also found that the Tribunal committed an error in not making calculation of the surplus available on the basis of the Full Bench Formula approved by this Court in the case of French Motor Car Co., Ltd. vs Workmen, ; , holding that there was a clear distinction between the two industries in the matter of payment of minimum wages and dearness allowance. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant company that the principle of fixing minimum wage had not been rigid and it was not necessary that the minimum should be fixed at the average level of wages prevailing in other comparable industries in that region, and that even if the workmen had not raised the plea that they were not comparable, no production bonus could be allowed to them. HELD: (i) The Tribunal committed a error of law requiring interference by this court in basing its decision on the principle contained in the earlier Agreement of 1959. [677 E] French Motor car Co., P. Ltd. & Anr. vs Its Workmen, , referred to. (ii)The Tribunal had directed that the increase in wages should be effective from April 1, 1958 and at least from June 30, 1963, there was not and there could possibly be a claim for higher bonus on the same basis as the permanent workers. [678 F] (iii)In the present case, the Tribunal had committed an erroneous error of fact in arriving at its decision. The claim for additional wages was based on the wage structure in the concern of the appellant and it had been accepted by mutual consent between the workmen and the company in an earlier settlement which had been arrived at in the year 1959. It was made clear that the dispute was raised by the workmen before the expiry of the year 1962 63. [679 G H] (iv)The claim for extra wages was not based on any material nor was it supported by any technical or badi workers. The award had to cover the year 1963 64 also and at the same time, the workmen would be entitled to bonus on that basis as in the other concerns. [680 D E] (v)In view of the finding of fact recorded by the Tribunal that there had been a very considerable rise in the price index and the labour had not so far raised a fresh dispute for a further revision of wages over and above the wages fixed by the tribunal which were being now refixed by this Tribunal, it was necessary to have a direction from this Court for fixing minimum wages on the present basis.

The appellant, a partnership firm, had constructed certain buildings on the land in question. The Income tax Officer issued to the assessee a notice under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961, for the assessment year 1960 61, and called upon him to produce before him its books of account and other relevant papers. The assessee filed his return of income as well as the relevant papers, but the Income tax officer did not accept the same. The order was challenged by the appellant in a writ petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the notice was invalid inasmuch as it did not comply with the requirements of section 151(2) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The report submitted by the Income Tax Officer to the Commissioner and the order of the Commissioner were not produced. [447 C] (ii) The return submitted by an assessee under section 149 was not a fit case for the issue of a notice tinder section 148. Therefore he could not have issued a notice, under section 151. Further his report did not mention any reason for coming to the conclusion that it was a fit cases for the issuance of a show cause notice under s.148. [449 E] (iii) The Commissioner had mechanically accorded permission and he did not himself record that he was satisfied that this was a case for investigating as to the truth of the alleged transactions. That is not the same thing as saying that there are reasons to issue, notice under sections 148.

The appellant, a firm carrying on business in Calcutta and Bombay, was assessed to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The income tax authorities held that the business carried on by the firm was carried on in Calcutta as a result of transfer of some of its businesses from other parts of India and that it had been carrying on the business in Calicut and Madras and that the income tax proceedings were barred by section 25(4) Of the Indian Incometax Act, 1918. The Appellate Tribunal held that there was no succession to the business and that there had been a discontinuance of the business as the business was carried out by two different firms and that therefore no new firm had been created. On reference, the High Court held that it was not necessary for the appellant to prove that there bad been a succession in Calcutta but only that the partnership was dissolved and that, consequently, the business continued in Calcutta even after 1948 so as to be continued under the Act of 1918. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The business which had been subjected to tax by section 26(2) Of Indian Income Tax Act, is not a dissolution of the firm but is merely a name to describe its partners compendiously, it is equally true that under the law of partnership the firm has no legal existence apart from its partners and it is merely one to describe their partners compendally. It is only if there was a discontinuance or a succession at an earlier period that the person succeeding should have succeeded his predecessor in carrying on that business as a whole. [117 E F] (ii) The mere change in the constitution of the partnership does not necessarily bring into existence a new assessable unit or a distinct assessable entity and in such a case there is no devolution of the, business as one of the partners cannot be removed to the notice of the point of view of succession because the identity of the person who owned it before and the identity is sought to be established by the partners as they liked without affecting the question of relief under section 25. [118 G H] (iii) The status of a firm is not to be taken to be disturbed by the coming in or going out of partners any more than that entity could be disturbed under the laws of Partnership. In other words, though a firm was to be regarded as an entity for the purpose of the Income tax law, that entity was not to he taken to have been disturbed by a subsequent change in its constitution. [119 G H; 120 A] (iv) The question whether there has been a partition or a mere change is essentially a question of fact and the High Courts would be reluctant to interfere with it unless it is shown that there has existed a succession.

The respondent, who was the karta of a Hindu Undivided Family, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of a 7/24th share in two houses. The appellant 's case was that the suit properties belonged to the joint family consisting of her husband and his two sons. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the properties belonged exclusively to the respondent and that there was no prior partition and that the plaintiff was entitled to a 7 /24th shares. On appeal, the High Court reversed the decree of the trial court and held that the property belonged to joint family and that it was not necessary for the plaintiff to prove his share in the joint Family properties. In appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: (1) The Hindu Succession Act came into force on June 17, 1956, Khandappa 's interest in the coparcenary property would devolve by survivorship upon the surviving members of the coparcenary and not in accordance with the provisions of the Act. But since the widow and daughter are amongst the female relatives specified in class I of the Schedule to the Act and Khandappa died leaving behind a widow and daughters, the proviso to section 6 comes into play and the normal rule is excluded. [766D E] (2) The Explanation to section six of the Hindu Successions Act does not provide further that in the circumstances therein stated, a notice under section 22 shall be deemed to have been issued and the notice shall be presumed not to have served on the deceased members of his sons. Whether a partition had actually taken place between the plaintiff 's husband and the two sons is beside the point for the purposes of Explanation 1. [769E F] (3) The proviso to s 6 does not require that a partition has in fact taken place before his death. It is not necessary, for the purpose of working out the fiction created by Explanation I to section 18A(9) that a share of the heirs must be ascertained on the basis that they bad separated from one another and had received a share in it. [759G H] (4) The interpretation which the statute requires to be made that a notice has in law been necessary to give its due and full effect as the fiction creates by section 18 A(9). [761A B] Shiramabai Bhimgonda vs Kalgonda, ; , referred to.

The Life Insurance Corporation of India (A.I.R.) Regulations, 1960 were framed under clauses (b) and (bb) of section 49(2) of the Life Insurance Act, 1956. Clause (b), inter alia, provided that the age of retirement of an employee shall be 60 years and upon his attaining the age Of 60 years he shall retire on completion of 58 years of age or at any time thereafter if his efficiency was found to have been impaired. The employees who joined the service after 1st September 1956 were transferred to the Corporation on or after 1th September 1956. In the case of those employees who had attained the age prescribed by Regulation 19(2), they were not entitled to continue in service beyond 58 years. The Corporation, however, issued a circular dated 9th June, 1966 which provided that "the age of superannuation of an officer of the Corporation shall be 55 years and on 1st Sept., 1956, the Executive Committee may at its discretion extend the service upto 60 years. " The employees of the Corpora tion were transferred from the Corporation to the Life Fund of the State of Orissa. The respondent who was employed in the Corporation as a daily rated employee, challenged the validity of Regulation 19 (2) and the circular on the ground that it violated the provisions of article 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the employees belonging to Class I and Class II were not governed by the Standing Orders and therefore they could not be reduced to 58 years only because they had been promoted to a class I post. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that since the respondent had been recruited originally into Class III service in 1976, he would have had the benefit of retire ment at the age upto 60 and hence his retirement could not have been reduced to 55 years only as he had been given the benefit thereof. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Standing Orders of 1960 as amended in 1977 and in clause (b)(bb) thereof provide that every ministerial railway servant who had entered the service on or before 31st March 1938 and who satisfied the conditions mentioned either in sub clauses (i) or (ii) thereof was entitled to be continued in service till he attained the ages of 60 years, provided they were otherwise eligible for re employment. [205E F] 2. The age of superannua tion is that of the employee on the basis of the date of entry into the service of the Government. It is not a matter of policy which has got to be decided by the Corporation and the Central Government. [206G] 3. The fact that an employee had entered service of a corporation after 1 September 1956 in a class III post and was later on promoted to Class II post does not make any difference in so far as the question which arises for decision before this Court is concerned.

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India with copies to the Prime Minister, Chief Justice of India and the Chief Jus tice of Punjab and Haryana High Court. The letter was signed by 15 members of the Bar belonging to District Bar Association, Bhiwani. In that letter they stated that if in view of this Hon 'ble Court the action of the deponent was not done he should prepare hisself for the commu nity. The appellants took a copy of their letter to Chief Justice and the same was endorsed by him on the same day. The High Court did not take any action against two persons on the letter written by them but only on a perusal of the contents thereof, held that the allegations in the letter were not disputed and challenged. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that there was no intention whatsoever on his part to scandalise the Hon ' ble High Court and if in the view of the High Court the allegation was brought personally by two members of Bar Association of Charkhi Dadri, Bhiwn to Chandigarh in a closed cover addressed to the Chief Justice for being handed over to him for his personal attention. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The contempt proceedings are dropped. [245E] 2. If on facts it appears that the Judge did say things or matters about politics such utterances or views or observations will be the personal opinions expressed by the Judge and therefore, the protec tive umbrella of the Court cannot be used by way of bringing the critics on the charge of contempt of court. [246E] 3. The matter did not constitute any contempt. The question whether the appellants committed any contempt of Court does not come up for consideration in this Court. [247B] 4. If the speech of any Judge is criticised and if it becomes a disputed question of fact as to whether any Judge did speak or not as is alleged by the writer, the matter would have to be ascertained by the court on facts whether the Judge concerned did speak on the matters ascribed to him before the Court. It is no part of the duty of a Judge nor is it a duty in discharge of office of a judge to go and address a meeting on political matters to redress grievances of the people. [243E F] 5. If, on facts, it appears from facts that the Judges did say anything or matters over political issues or views of the matter or to concern themselves with political issues, or policies under taken by political parties as a part of their political programme, the Judge cannot in such a case take shelter behind his office if the public discusses and criticises the views expressed by him. [244B C] 6. If an speech of a member is criticised, and if the speech is criticised it becomes the disputed question or any matter to concern himself with political issue or to concerns themselves with legislative issues or policies. [242C D] 7. The Court cannot in the instant case take advantage behind his official system of Government.

The petitioner was a member of the Indian Income tax Investigation Commission. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of section 5(1) of the Act on the ground that it violated article 14 of the Constitution and was therefore violative of equal protection of laws and that the provisions of section 6(4) of Act XXX of 1947 were based on a valid classification which was based on intelligible differentia. The petitioner contended that the procedure prescribed by the impugned Act for discovering the concealed profits of certain companies had been violated inasmuch as the Commission had not given any opportunity to the petitioner to meet the evidence and that there was no substantial difference between the two procedures laid down in section 5 (1) and section 5 of the impugned act. Held, that the impugned provisions were valid and did not contravene article 14 Of the Constitution. The procedure prescribed under the Act for ascertaining whether concealed profits had been disclosed by the petitioner was substantially different from that adopted in section 6 of the , and the procedure followed by the Commission was substantially prejudicial to the assessee than the procedure laid down by the Indian Incometax Act. Held further, that section 5 was not violative of article 14 as it did not provide any adequate treatment for the loss suffered by the assessee. The provisions of sections 6 and 7 of the said Act were in no way inconsistent with the provisions contained in section 34 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and were therefore void and unenforceable. The impugned Act contravened article 14 and was, therefore, void. Held also, that it was not necessary to decide whether section 5 had been complied with by the Investigation Commission or not as there was nothing in the Act which would justify the conclusion that the investigation was vitiated for any reason whatsoever.

The appellant, a company registered under the Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on business as a "commercial establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954. The main object of the Federation was to establish a Trust or Trusts and to provide for certain matters connected therewith. Section 2(1)(a) of that Act defines " commercial establishment" to mean any premises where goods are sold either by retail or wholesale or where services are rendered to customers, and includes an office, a warehouse, a shop, a commercial establishment, residential hotel, restaurant, eating houses, hotels, etc., and other establishments in which business of banking, insurance, stocks, busi ness, residential hotels, clubs, restaurants, eating house, theatre, or other places of public amusement or entertainment. The appellant was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act 1913. It had its registered office at Kanpur and New Delhi. The Federation was a " commercial Establishment" within section 2 (5) Of the Act. The respondent, a Company registered under section 26 of the Act, was a commercial Establishment within the definition of "commercial establishments". The appellant contended that it was not an establishment as defined in section 2 of the . The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the activity amounted to "business" and that the activities of the appellant were not "a commercial establishment", and that there was no "establishment" as defined under section 2. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The definition of 'commercial establishment ' in section2(5), includes a "shop". A place in order to fall within the term "commercial Establishment" must be "premises". Secondly, it should be premises wherein (a) any trade, business or profession is carried on, or (b) any work in connection therewith or incidental thereto is carried out. Sub clause (b), is only ancillary to (a). There is no doubt that the registered office of the respondent was premises. The controversy centres round the question whether the activity of the Association amounted to a "business or trade" within Section 2 (1)(d) of The Delhi Shops & Establishments Act 1954. [356D E] (2) It is well settled that a systematic activity can be a business activity even if no dividends are declared or profits shared. In the matter of Incorporated Council of Law Reporting for England and Wales, (3) The Federation also publishes periodicals, bulletins etc. and issues the same to member free of this Court in R. K. Mittal 's case. [355F G] (4) It will bear repetition that the Federation also published periodicals and other publications relating to legal subjects. In carrying them out the association employed editors, reporters, printers etc., it is not distributed among its members. But that does not alter the "fact that its activity is a trading or business activity". For all the foregoing reasons particularly in view of the decision of this court in R K. Pandi 's Case, (supra), the High Court was right in holding that there is no "business", trade or profession within the purview of Section 2.(5) and that it cannot be said that the commercial or industrial exhibitions run by a society is directly or substantially in issue in R . K. Batra 's ease. [354G H] (5)(a).

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family consisting of his two brothers and the Karta. The income from the property in question was assessed to agricultural income tax under the Income tax Act, 1922. The assessee received a sum of Rs. 36,396/ as an allowance for the life time of the Jagirdar who had been granted a sanad of Rajasree. The amount was determined at Rs.36,396. The Income tax Officer held that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income. He accordingly disallowed the claim of the appellant. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income Tax Officer. The High Court in reference under section 66A(2) of the Act answered the question in the negative. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The source of income is clearly the arrangement arrived at in 1837 and therefore it is not agricultural income as defined in the Act. [707 D] (a) If it is held in this case that the source of allowance or pension was the arrangement, arrived at, in 1838, then the income cannot be held to be derived from land within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii). The source will be different if he exchanges (1)[1915] A.C. 1104 Narain Singh vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bihar and Orissa, [1955] 1 S.C R. 603, followed. (b) In the present case the source will not arise out of the financial point of view. The allowance is revenue income and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income under section 4 (3)(vii). [708 D E] (c) If the assessee 's predecessor had received compensation for relinquishing his title to the lands in dispute, that would have been a capital receipt and not taxable. [0709 G] (d) The allowance was revenue income. The fact that the income of a Hindu Undivided Family was clearly the agreement arrived at between the parties did not lead to the inference that by this settlement contained in the letter dated July 7, 1837, the source would be the arrangement. [0810 B C] (e) If there is no material on record to show that the allowance was in fact a payment in instalments of the value of the disputed title of the assesses 's father 's successor in interest, the income could not be held liable to tax.

The petitioners in Civil Appeal No. 441 of 1981 were working as Chargeman Grade II in the various departments of the State of Madhya Pradesh. In the year 1962, the Assam Government issued a notification dated 6th November 1962 under Rule 8 of the Rules framed by the President of India for promotion to the post of Chargeman II in all the three wings of the Department of Defence Production and Excer tively, the said posts were redes sary to be filled up by direct recruitment and by promotion from Grade II. The petitioners in C.A. No. 442 of 1981 had been working as Supervisor 'A ' on the basis of a selection list prepared for the different grades by duly constituted Depart ment in accordance with the said Rules. In pursuance of the said order, the respond ents issued an advertisement dated 6 th November 1962 inviting applications from eligible candidates for promotion as Chargemen Grade II and in the said notification it was mentioned that the selection list was to be made on the recommendation of the Departmental Promotion Committee. The names of the petitioners were also sent for consideration by the Departmental Promotee. In a writ petition filed by them, the High Court decided the Writ Petition in favour of the appel lants holding that the direction given by the Court had not been complied with and that the appellants were entitled to be promoted as Charge man Grade II on completion of 2 years ' service by duly consid ered Selection Committee.

The respondent State Transport Authority issued a notification under section 63(7) of the , authorising the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation to grant certain additional stage carriage permits to private operators and increased the number of permits granted to the Indian Tourism Development Corporation. The appellant State Road Trans port Corporation, which was a public sector undertaking, challenged the grant of three out of eleven permits to its non preferable operator and increased their number by adding one more application for renewal of the same. The High Court allowed the writ petitions on the ground that the preference contemplated by the proviso to section 63 (7) was not violative of article 14 of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court were wrong in distinguishing the decision of this Court in Sher Singh vs Union of India, ; and that the true position was that on a correct interpretation of the proviso, the preference became operative only if other things were equal. HELD: (i) The scheme excludes omnibus operators and requires applicants to have either two years ' experience in the car hire business with contacts in the tourist business or to own five tourist taxies. There are no guidelines as to how the discretion to grant approval is to be exercised once the minimum conditions are fulfilled. [1019C D] Sher Singh & Ors. vs Union, of India; , ; and Sher Singh V Union of lndia, ; , referred to. (ii) The High Courts have failed to consider the merits of the claims of the Karnataka state Road Transport Corpora tion and the private operators who did not get a certificate of approval from the Central Government because of the rule of preference contained in proviso to Section 63( 7).

The respondent purchased a business carried on by the appellant under the name and liabilities of the respondent. The business was transferred to the respondent in 1956. The respondent paid some amounts towards sales tax and claimed that the amount should be paid in such manner and in such instalments, if any, within 30 days of the transfer. The Sales Tax authorities took the view that Rule 21 A of the Sales Tax Rules was illegal and ultra vires and the respondent was not liable to pay the sales tax due from him. The appellant appealed to the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that Rule21 A was ultra vires of the rule making power of the State Government under section 19(1) and 19(2)(c) of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Rule 21A is beyond the rule made power of State Government either under section 9 or section 19 (2)(C) of Act. It was then submitted by the respondent that Rule 1 A was intra vires of it and the High Courts were not justified in interfering with the order of the subordinate authorities. [665 E F] Badridas Daga vs C.I.T., Bihar, ; , referred to. (ii) The word "assessment" used in section 19 of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1939 does not include the power of recovering tax assessed from a person other than the assessee. It follows therefore that Rule 23 A is beyond question for the period with which it was made by the State Legislature. [664 F] (iii) Rule 22A is ultra vires as it was not open to the State Govt. to rely on the instrument inter vivos between the transferor and the transferee and to contend that there is a liability created inter se between the State Govern ment on the one hand and the transferor on the other. To put it differently, it is not open for the State Gov ernment to rely upon the instrument Inter vivo ny between the transferee on the contrary. [663 G] Badrinas Daga V C. I.T.

The respondent was appointed senior jailor, Surendranagar District Jail. He was suspended and later on served with a charge sheet. In the departmental inquiries held against him he was found guilty of misconduct under section 5(2) (a) of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, 1960. The trial court dismissed his suit holding that the order of dismissal was illegal and void. On appeal the District Judge confirmed the decision of the trial court but on second appeal the High Court set aside the decree of the lower appellate court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the High Courts erred in holding that there had been a breach of article 311(2), of the Constitution as the respondent was not concerned with the second contention; (2) the charge against the appellant was not a liability arising out of a contract but was a liability in respect of an actionable wrong other than breach of contract, and (3) the order passed by the lower Appellate Court was illegal. HELD: The appeal must be dismissed. (i) The respondent was entitled under the Workmen 's Compensation Act to compensation from the shipowners not only in respect Of his wages but also of the retainer which must be taken into account as earnings under a concurrent contract of service. [923 B] In the instant case, the appellant had been assessed to the satisfaction of the Government and that was made as a result of the said enquiry. The respondent could not therefore be held guilty of non supply of the report of the Enquiry Officer. [936 C D] (ii) The High Court erred in setting aside the order on the ground that the failure on the part of the competent authority to provide the appellant with a copy of the enquiry report was not fatal to the non supply. [981 E F] State of Bihar vs Abdul Majid, ; , referred to.

The appellant was the owner of a coal mine. The respondent 's land was leased to one Walji Kheta in 1945 for mining coal from the encroached portion of the appellant 's colliery. The lease deed provided that the lessee would not be entitled to any compensation for any damage caused by the use of coal without his consent and that the lessees would not take possession of the same. The appellant claimed that the intermediate boundary line between the two leaseholds was a part of the original lease deed, and that it was a portion of mauza Kujama and the western boundary was shown as the eastern boundary of the respondent 'Sangji Khet. The trial court held that the respondent had encroached upon the appellant "in the land in dispute" and that by virtue of section 3 Of the Indian , the appellant had failed to prove that the respondents had knowledge of the obstruction caused to the appellant by the encroachment. On appeal, the High Court reversed the finding of the Subordinate Judge and dismissed the suit. Held, that the High court was right in holding that the burden of proof lay on the respondent to prove the fact that he had knowledge about the encroachment only within three years of the suit, and the onus of proof being on the appellant, the onus was upon the respondent who asserts a right and it may be having regard to the circumstances of each case that the onus is on him. The burden of proving the fact which lies on the plaintiff in these suits to prove affirmatively the knowledge of his possession of his occupation of the converted property and that he has to prove such knowledge by evidence. Held further, that under section 101 of the Indian Evidence Act, the burden is upon the plaintiff to prove not merely that the property was in his possession but to allege the date when they had knowledge or had knowledge thereof. The onus of proving facts which lay on a person who substantially asserts the affirmative of the issue is certainly on the respondents. The rule of construction of statutes is applicable only where there is an essential distinction between the phrase "burden of proof" as a matter of law and pleading and as a matters of adducing evidence. Darapali Sadagar vs Najir Ahmed, Pat. 312, approved.

The appellant was a crosscutter. He was charged with having committed an offence under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders without holding any departmental inquiry and the order was communicated to him by the same day. The appellant contended that it was entitled under r, 18(b) of that standing orders to dispense with the service of any employee after complying with its terms. Held, that the employer could not be allowed to defend the action under r., 18 (a). The Standing Orders in this case were framed by the Labour Appellate Tribunal for adjudication and there was nothing for it to justify before the tribunal in the manner indicated above. The Industrial Tribunal had occasion to consider this matter relating to discharge by notice or in lieu thereof by payment of wages for a certain period without assigning any reason. Buckingham and Carnatic Co. Ltd. vs Workers of the Company, ; , referred to. Held further, that it is not correct to say that the Industrial Court could inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of service even under a rule like 18(c) of Standing Orders. Butifyingham and carnatic Cooperative Society Employees ' Union, Bombay vs The Chartered Bank Employees ' Association, ; and Bharat Bank Ltd. Patna vs Bali Rai, [1962] 2 S.C.R. 829, referred to, Held further that the Tribunal had rightly held that the exercise of power was colourable exercise of the power under that rule in as much as that rule was used to get rid of an employee instead of following the course of holding an inquiry for misconduct, notice for which had been given to the employee and for which a departmental enquiry was intended to be held.

The appellant filed a suit against the receivers of the owners and on August 19, 1954, the receivers granted a lease of the theatre to the latter on certain terms and conditions. The appellant contended that the agreement dated November 27, 1954 was not a lease but only a lease. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the question whether the agreement between the plaintiff and defendant Nos. 5 and 6 was a commercial transaction and was not an "lease" within the meaning of section 28 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947. The High Court in revision set aside the decree holding that it was not open to the trial court to decide whether the document dated November 26, 1954 created a lease or not. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether a party is entitled to lead evidence or to put questions in cross examination of the plaintiff 's witnesses cannot form the subject matter of an issue. [439 B] (ii) A consent decree does not operate as res judicata because a consent decree is merely the record of a contract between the parties to a suit, to which is superadded the seal of the Court.
