A matter in contest in a suit may operate as a bar of res judicata as far as the question of document of November 27. 1954, creatin g a lease is concerned. The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. This Court has recorded a finding that the consent decree was merely the recording of a formal agreement arising out of the agreement. [441 G H] (iii) A compromise decree, accord ingly, does not operates as resjudicata because a joint application of the parties and a consent order is merely a decision on any of the issues. But the expression " case" is restricted to the entire suit in dispute and not a part of the proceeding imposes an unwarranted restriction on the exercise of powers of superintendence and may result in certain cases in denying relief to the aggrieved party where it is most needed and may cause injury to the affected litigant where it was most needed, and may be result in the perpetration of gross injustice. But it was for the trial Court in the first instance to decide that question and there after the High Court could, if the matter were brought before it by way of appeal or revision, have decided that question. [442 E F] Major section section Khanna vs Brig. F. J. Dillon ; , referred to.

The respondent was appointed as a pilot Officer in the Indian Air Force on contract basis for a fixed term which could be extended from time to time subject to the suitability of the official concerned but not beyond 58 years of age. The appellant, who was an employee of the respondent Board, was terminated by the issue of a notice and payment of one month 's salary. The order was challenged before the High Court in a Writ Petition on the ground that the order of termination was not in the nature of a contract and as such could not be sustained. The High Court held that the termination order could not he sustained and quashed the order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was entitled to be reinstated in service irrespective of the fact whether the Governor had extended the period of his appointment beyond 30th August, 1985. Allowing the Appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in disposing of the Writ Petition as it did on 24.3.1988. [243D] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent had not urged before the Single Judge that the interim order that had been passed on 10.7.86 entitled him to be re instated in service even though there was no order of extension of service. If the respondent is really aggrieved by the Judgment dated 24. 3.1988 he should have preferred an appeal before this Court and that did not do but on the other hand he proceeded to file a Review Petition claiming to be reinstatement in service on the slender ground that he was entitled for salary upto 30th of August,1985 if the order was found to be an invalid one. [242E F] 1:3. The respondent was employed only under a contract which specified the term of his appoint ment which extended only upto 30st of August 1985.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the evidence of the eye witnesses was not sufficient to convict him as they were interested in the incident and that the discrepancies noticed by the Sessions Judge were of a minor character and that they had been unduly magnified by the learned Sessions Judge. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High court was justified in interfering with the order of acquittal merely because another view is also possible. [368E] (2) It is well settled that at one time it was thou nt that an order of conviction could be set aside for "substantial and compelling reasons" only and Courts used to launch on a search to discover those "substantial & compelling reasons". However, the circumstances were possible on the evidence and the accused was entitled to the benefit of doubt arising from the two views and that where the Trial Court has taken a possible view and acquitted the accused, the High Court should not interfere with the acquittal merely on the ground that another view was also possible.[368F H] Sanwat Singh & Ors. vs State of Rajasthan, ; , followed. (3) The discrepancies were in regard to which of them woke up first, where was the lantern and which of the neighbours came first to the scene on hearing their cries. The witnesses were of such a nature that they could have been seen by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. He probably attributed the refusal to reluctance on the part of his wife to accompany him straightaway. [369A B] Sanwar Singh & ors. vs The State of Bihar, ; and Sanwat Sing & Ors., vs State, A.l. R. , referred to. (4) In the instant case, the evidence was corroborated by the evidence given by the prosecution witnesses. It is true that the accused did not have any deep motive to kill the deceased. It was obvious that he must have been upset by the constant refusal of brother and her mother to send the deceased with him for a thumb impression on which the deceased was sleeping. The evidence of P. Ws. 4 and 5 who came to the spot soon afterwards, could not be said to have been caused in the manner suggested by the accused. [370E F] Sanat Singh & Anr.

The appellant, a Judge of the Supreme Court, was appointed as a Judge in the High Court of Madhya Pradesh. He was placed under suspension on the ground that he had been committed to the offence of criminal misconduct under section 5(1)(e) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The charge sheet submitted by the Chief Justice of India against him was served on him on the basis of a report made by the Judge of Supreme Court in which he stated that he was not in possession of disproportionate assets disproportionate to his known sources of income. He also stated that the Chief justice or the State Government had been authorised to remove a Judge from his office and to maintain the rule of law, even though the Chief Justices of India were not empowered to remove him from his duties except by taking recourse to procedure prescribed under section 6(1) (c) of Act. The appellant contended that he should be given an opportunity of being heard before any action could be taken against a Judge who was in possession or had been found guilty of criminal charge under section 161(4) of Indian Penal Code, and that the Central Government or the state Government or any other authority could not have intended to act on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the appellant was entitled to a hearing as provided by section 6 (1)(c) and that he would be immune from prosecution in respect of acts done by him. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the President of India had not been authorised by law to act upon the aid or advice of his Council of ministers with the Chief Minister of the State, and as such the Central Legislature was competent to appoint and to remove the Judge. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of clauses (4) and (5) of Article 124 of the Constitution are not intended to be covered by the Act. [297G] 2.1 The power conferred on the President under clause (c), is subject to the provisions of the Act, except in connection with his removal from office in the manner prescribed. Clause (e) has to be read as a part of the scheme under which the public servant is required to furnish particulars of his assets with reference to which the disproportion and his inability to satisfactorily account can be inferred. The ambit and scope of the enactment is to be determined on the true construction of the provisions contained in clauses (a), (b) and(c) as contemplated by Article 124(4). [297H; 298A] 2:2.1 In the case of a public servant who commits an offence under section 16(1), he has to furnish his account of assets with the previous sanction of the competent authority before removing him from office. The competent authority can form the requisite opinion on the question whether the holder of a post is liable to be removed from his service by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a minority of not less than two thirds members of that Assembly present and voting. [298B C] 2(a) The power to remove an Judge of a High Court or the Supreme court under clause(4), is not confined to cases where the President has the power to hold office as held in the case, but whose category for the grant of sanction for prosecution is not envisaged by section six(b). [298C] (b)(i) The word 'suit ' in clause (e), in the context of which it is used, must be given a wider meaning and should be construed in the light of the object of the statute. In other words, if the holder has the right to hold an office as a public officer he may be prosecuted without sanction under section six or sub section (2) of section 5 of the .

The appellant was a member of the Sahas ' community specified in item 40 of the Schedule to the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The respondent filed an election petition challenging the validity of the appellant 's election on various grounds. The High Court held that the appellant belonged to the "Scheduled Caste" specified in Item 40 and therefore was not a member belonging to the Scheduled Caste specified in items 40 and 42 for the purpose of the Constitution. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Tribunal had gone wrong in considering the Saha 's case as an independent caste. It had taken the same view. [391 C] (ii) The finding that the respondent belonged to a smaller caste group within the bigger caste group of Sunri caste was altogether irrelevant to the point in issue. Evidence cannot alter the natural interpretation of the words in the Order. For the same reason, the Tribunal 's conclusion that the Saha s ' included the Saha as a member is correct. [390 G] (iii) The High Courts were in error in interpreting the item on the evidence in the case as they appear to have done. [392 C D] (iv) The respondent called witnesses to establish that the appel lant belonged to "Scheduled caste" and not a 'Scheduled Caste". The Tribunal was therefore right in holding that the charge against the appellant was proved. [393 G H] (v) If the intention was to exclude from Sunri Caste certain persons who bore the surname Saha, the Order would have made that clear. In the absence of such words "UBren" must be understood as referring to a larger caste group. It is legitimate to think that if the excluded Sahas were those Sunri and other characteristics within the smaller caste groups of Sunra District which had been transferred to West Bengal were not to be considered as belonging to a Scheduled Caste, the order expressly says so.

The appellant was the tenant of a flat on the second floor of a building in which he had a share. The tenancy was a monthly one and the rent being Rs. 215 per month, the rent was paid by the complainant to the appellant. The appellant asked for a certificate under article 134(1)(c) of the Constitution to show that the offence arose only on receipt of any sum or consideration as a condition for the relin quishment of his tenancy. Held, that an assignment of the lease or transfer in any other manner by a tenant is not made an offence; the statute merely says that it is not a lawful transaction and does not require any arrangement to pay rent for relinquishment of the tenancy of any premises. The words "the relinquishment of tenancy of a premises by a tenants" in section 108(1) of Transfer of Property Act, are not intended to be confined only to the transfer by a lessee or tenant of his interest as such. The consent of the landlord to an assignment is not necessary in the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary. In the case of relinquishment it cannot be a unilateral transaction; it can only be in favour of the lessor by mutual agreement between them. The intention of the legislature to grant a lease must be to the lessor or one who holds his interest. The permission of the Rent Controller to an assigned of a lease by sub lease or otherwise on receipt Of consideration that has been made an offi cution. The section does not speak of relinquishment or giving up of possession,in general terms. The word "relinquishment" does not occur in the Transfer of property Act but it is found in many of the Tenancy Acts in various provinces where there are sections 14 and 18 of the Transfer o f Property Act.

The appellant company was a divisional undertaking and its workmen were paid dearness allowance at 10% of the basic pay. The company had its own depots in Delhi and other places. The employees of the company were paid wages at the rate of 30% of basic pay, dearness allowance and house rent allowance. The Company made an application before the Tribunal under Rule 31 of the Industrial Disputes (Bombay) Rules, 1957 for a modification of the existing scales of pay with flat rates of Rs. 150/ and Rs. 100/ in the case of other categories. The Tribunal held that the company was unable to rely on the new scale of dearness allowance as it had not been included in the basic wage structure. On appeal by the workmen, the Tribunal held: (1) that the appellant was a separate class industry and not a manufacturing concern; (2) that it was bound by the order made under Rule 32 of the industrial Disputes ( Bombay) Rules 1957; (3) that there was no justification for revising the existing scale of Dearness Allowance. The appellant company appealed to this Court against the Tribunal 's judgment. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Tribunal had given a clear finding on the question whether the company could bear the additional financial burden. At the end of paragraph 15 of the Award the Tribunal stated that it would be necessary for the Tribunal to modify the existing structure with suitable increments provided therein. [179F] 1.2 In the instant case, the Industrial Tribunal has not given any reasons for quashing the order dated December 22, 1978 of the Tribunal. The omission of the words to each employee first after the figure Rs.150/ and again after the figures Rs.100/ was clearly an accidental slip or omission which the Tribunal was entitled to correct. [180G] 1:3. The corrigendum was in effect a fresh award. The additional financial liability should be revised accordingly. [181H; 182A] 1.(a) The corrigendum is not a new wage bill, and the scales of dearness pay are being revised with suitable amendments subsequently made consequent thereto. [182B] (b) The Tribunal has given satisfactory reasons for adopting a different mode and it is not possible to maintain one part of the award and supersede another. It cannot be doubted that an Industrial Tribunal deciding upon the wage scales of the employees of an establishment would have full liberty to propose ad hoc increase of salaries as part of its revision of wages. Nor can it be doubted whether any problem would arise for interpretation of the order. [183C D] (c) The additional burden is on the appellant to show that the corrigendum was not justified. [184D E] (d) The amendment of the new structure by prescribing a ceiling on dearness allowance or scale of pay, and making it clear that the basic principle of dearness payment would be to apply to each individual case. [185E F] (e) The change in the award of the appellant 's existing wage scales is not the giving of any ad hoc enhancement of salaries. It is only a revision of the scales with flat rise in the number of pay packet whereas the junior employees would get a large benefit. While workmen raising industrial disputes for revision of wage scales are certainly minded about their future prospects in the matter of wages, they surely would be more concerned with the immediate benefits according to them that is why it would obviously result in serious anomalous situations. [186F G] (f) The new award has been made a supplementary award which has not been challenged. The amendment introduced by the new award was only an additional charge and not an additional demand of salary for 150/or Rs. 50/ per day. The addition of Rs, 150/ in other categories is clearly an additional wage structure with a view to neutralise a portion of increase in the cost of living index. [187G H] (g) The amendments introduced by Act No.

The respondent, an award made by the Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/ per day and in pursuance thereof, the management of the appellant company had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the award. This agreement was subsequently published in the Bihar Gazette as a part of the award, and in spite of the Award and the agreement, the appellant paid its employees only As. /10/ per month and that led to the present claim made by them under section 15 of the Act. The respondents contended before the Tribunal that the refusal of the appel lant to pay to them wages at the rate awarded, in substance amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant to pay the said prescribed wages. The Tribunal held that section 2(vi) includes wages prescribed by an award could not be included as wages under section 2 (vi). On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act are applicable only to the payment of wages fixed by an order in an industrial dispute between the employer and his employees. If it is shown to the satisfaction of the Tribunal, that the terms of contract of employment for instance need to be revised in the interests of social justice, it is at liberty to consider the matter, take into account all relevant factors and if a change or revision of the terms appears to be justified, it can and often enough it does radically change the terms Of the contract of service. (ii) The development of industrial law during the last decade bears testimony to the fact that on references made under section 10(1) of the , the said awards supplant contractual terms in respect of matters covered by them and are substituted for them. That being so, it was difficult to accede to the argument that the wages prescribed must be paid by industrial adjudication. (iii) The award cannot be treated as wages in lieu of wages under s 2(iv).

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was put up for trial under section 465 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and tried by a Special judge. The prosecution case was that there was an application by the Department for sanction to prosecute the appellant for an offence under section 409, Indian Penal Code, for forging thumb impression of a person in charge of certain works at a place called Karhali. The sanction was granted on the ground that the official capacity was involved in the very act complained of as amounting to a crime and that he had committed MIS misappropriation. The Special judge held that the prosecution was bad for want of sanction, but the High Court held that it was necessary to sanction under section 197(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code, because, the appellant did not claim to have spent the amount in the course of his official duties, and accordingly convicted him under section 466, Indian penal Code. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the conviction of the appellant was illegal as he had failed to prove that the offence of criminal misappropriation or forgery had been brought home to the appellant or not. The absence of sanction is fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. Hori Ram Singh vs Emperor (1949) L.R. 75 I.A. 185, approved. The King vs B. Gill and Another (1948) L R. 75 1. A. 180, disapproved. The question whether a criminal breach of trust can be committed while purporting to act in execution of his duty as a public servant depends upon the facts of each case. H. H., B. always referred to the facts and circumstances of each particular case.

The assessee was a banking company incorporated in the State of Cochin with branches in that State. It carried on business in Travancore and other States. The income tax authorities determined its assessable income to be Rs. 90,947 representing only the profit it made in Travancore State and under section 32(1) proviso (i) of the Travancore Income tax Act, 1922, the assessee was assessed under the Indian Income tax Rules, 1922. In the assessment for the year 1950 51 the assessee claimed that the business losses incurred in Travancore should be set off against the profits of Travancore State. The claim was disallowed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal on appeal. On reference the High Court held that the banking business of the assessee being one and indivisible for the purpose of determining the amount assessable to income tax it was entitled to deduct the losses incurred outside Travancore State from the profits accruing in Travancore, State and other Indian States. In appeal to this Court by special leave: HELD : The question referred to the High court was answered in favour of the Revenue. It is a fundamental rule of construction that a proviso must be considered with regard to the principal matter to which it stands as proviso. Therefore, it is not necessary for the Tribunal to determine the true meaning of the main enactment by providing an exception and taking out as it were from the main Act, a portion which, but for the proviso would fall within the main section. [267 D E] The Commissioner of Income tax vs Shaw Wallace & Co., Ltd., ; , relied on. In re: Hingorani Textiles Co. Ltd., and Inland Revenue Co. vs Commissioners of Inland Revenue, , referred to.

The appellant company was incorporated in January 1946 as a Private Limited Company. The Head Office of the Company is at Calcutta and the General practice of the company both at the Head Office and the Branch Offices appears to have been to retire its employees at the age of 55 though in certain cases the company in its discretion permitted an employee to continue beyond that age. In September 1959, an agreement was entered into between the company and its employees for the Calcutta employees ' retirement age at 60. The terms of the agreement were: " That the age Of retirement shall be 58 years in accordance with the provisions of the Pension Insurance Scheme for employees generally or for industrial employees and under social assistance or universal schemes in forty eight countries in 1954, but the Company may in its option, and with the express or implied consent of the employee concerned continue an employee after he attains that age". The appellant company claimed that it was agreeable to introduce for its Bombay employees provisions similar to those which had been introduced by agreement for the purpose of Calcutta employees retirement at the rate of 58 years. The Tribunal held that the age was fixed at 60 and not at 60, but on a closer examination of the evidence on record, it found that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay region there was no indication at all as to how long ago the age should be fixed at 55. On appeal by the workmen, this Court, HELD: (1) The Tribunal had rightly rejected their claim for fixing the age at 58 years and not on the basis of any previous findings. [426 B] (2) The approach adopted by the Tribunal was wrong in its view that what was said by itself on an earlier occasion and was confirmed by this Court in appeal, was in fact inaccurate. [427 C D] (3) There is no indication in the evidence that the trend in Bombay Region had been to fix the retirement age of clerical and subordinate staff at 60 years. It is not clear from the evidence as to what long ago it was so fixed at 58 or at 58. The statement filed by the appellant company before the Tribunal that the previous decisions were to fix their retirement age for 60 years, was wholly insufficient to indicate any slowing down of this trend. [ 428 E F] (4) There was no reason why these concerns should not be accepted as correct. [527 C D].

The appellant company was incorporated in the year 1961 and its principal object was to carry on business of manufacturing and selling textiles. It had an authorised capital of Rs. 1,00,000 shares of Rs, 100 each. The appellant company had also been appointed a Director of the Company. In the course of which it had also appointed a number of directors. On May 10, 1965, the Board of Directors of the company passed a resolution to take action under section 237(b) of the , for the removal of the Chairman and the other members of the Board. The Board was to send its report to the Board in September 1964. In October 1964, the appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court challenging the order of the board appointing the directors as directors on the ground that the Board had acted mala fide in their conduct and that the Chairman alone acted without jurisdiction. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the power delegated to it by section 237 (b) was not unguided, uncontrolled or uncanalised but was only subject to control by the Board under section 235(b). In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The power conferred on the Central Government by section 236(b), is of two kinds, namely, (i) calling for information or explanation from the company and (ii) ordering an investigation into the affairs of a company. [342 G] (2) The powers are discretionary and its exercise depends upon the honest formation of opinion that an investigation is necessary. It must be exercised by the Central Govt. in the interest of the general public. If the power conferred by section 235 is administrative, that would be the only thing to do so. [343 B C] (3) The order made by the Chairman on behalf of the appellant company is not invalid. The order was passed under section 236 (b). The order dated May 19, 1965 was passed by the Secretary of the Central Board in charge of the affairs and it could not be said that the order was invalid. [344 C] The power to issue a notification under section 239(b)(1) is an executive power and the control over the exercise of the delegated functions is retained by the nominee of Parliament, that is, the Central Govern ment. [345 E F] (4) The Board has power to constitute a company law board and to delegate its powers to it. It can also delegate its functions to itself. The power under section 234(b ) may be exercised only in the case of a sub inspector appointed by the Government. But, if the Board is entrusted with the power and functions of the sub inspector, it must be presumed that each member of the committee should exercise his individual judgment on the matter and all, the members of such committee should act together and arrive at a joint decision. [346 G H] (5) The delegation of powers by section 239 (b)(i) to the Central government is not an administrative power but it sets out the circumstances that may be taken into consideration. [347 B C; 347 A] (6) The Central Government has under sections 10, 11 and 12 power to frame rules regulating the procedure of the directors and to issue licences for the conduct of the business of the respondent company. The Central Governme nt has power under s.234(b); it is not competent to them to delegate their functions to the board. [349 C D] (7) The Chairman, in his affidavit, stated that he had no power to appoint any person as inspectors and that he did not have any such powers.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence to one year 's rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100/ . In appeal to this Court it was contended that the presumption that they were dacoits ought not to have been drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case, because dacoity as such is not challenged before this Court. HELD : The law advocated by Mr. Chari is not correct. If there is other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small the finding of the stolen property with him is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence. There is then no question of presumption. The evidence corroborating the other evidence already against him is sufficient to prove that he was concerned with the murder. [724 D E] In what circumstances the one presumption or the other may be drawn, it is not necessary to state categorically in this case. It all depends upon the circumstances under which the discovery of the fruits of crime are made with a particular accused. It has been stated on more than one occasion that if the gap of time is too large the presumption should be drawn. [624 D] In the present case, the goods stolen were not sold and were being taken back to the dealers by the cartmen. A large number of persons said to be 20 in number pelted stones at the cart men and looted the property. Immediately afterwards a number of searches were made and the goods were found with various persons who were prosecuted as offenders. The houses of 20 persons were searched and large quantities of the theft goods were recovered from them. It is impossible to think that within the short time available, these goods could have been easily disposed of to receivers of stolen property or could be placed in the custody of friends till such time as the original offenders could take them away.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of "Tolinner" within the meaning of Section 5 of the , filed writ petitions in this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the vires of section 5 of Act XIII of 1919 (the Act) and for a direction to the State Government to include therein the substance as poison for purposes of restriction to be imposed on the possession of "unit is a manufacturing only those thinners which contain only liquid substance" like "discretions harmless in themselves". The petitioners contended that since the Act was a Central enactment it was possible of unjust and unjustified discrimination as it was left to each State Government, to determine what substance they would include as poison and regulated and the decision in one State to include the substance was unreasonable. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of neither Section 2 nor 5 nor the impugned notification are hit by any consti tutional limitation. [223E] 2. The Act is intended to regulate the importation, possession and sale of poisons. Some substances which the Government consider its possession for sale or sale to be regulated in the interest of health and safety of the society. This limitation is inherent in the scheme of the Act itself. Of course no comprehensive definition can be given to the word poison. Under this term it nobody can be considered to have an absolute right to carry on any trade or business. [222F] 3. The nature of trade in poison is such that nobody can he considered to be a poison for the entire country. The notification and its application to any area would depend on the necessity to declare the substance which would include "phenches of life". [223G] 4. Section 2(3) enables the Government by Rule to regulate possession, sale and sale in that area. It is a busi ness which can be termed even as inherently dangerous to health and fire safety of society in view of the rampant misuse and sale to the poor, weak and helpless as an intoxicant. A law in such circumstances can regulate the trade. This pos session is well settled and it would be pedantic to cite all the authorities of this Court on this point. [224H; 223A] 5. The Notification and its applica tion to any areas would depend upon the necessity for declaring the substance, as poison on the particular facts and situation prevailing in that locality and the need to regu lates the possession and sell ment of the same. No question of discrimination can arise in such circum stances. [225B] 6. The provision of neither section 2 nor5 nor the order are hit either by any provi sional limitation or is violative of any right to trade. [226C] 7. The writ petition accordingly fails and it is dismissed.

The appellant firm carried on business in drugs, chemicals, mercury, camphor and silk yam and as money lenders. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim of the assessee holding that the debt did not arise in the course of money lending business but was in respect of loans made in the ordinary course of such business. On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner agreed with the Income tax officer. The Tribunal, however, held that the debts were mere accommodations which could have no bearing to the regular business carried on by the assessee and therefore the disallowance of bad debt was right. In reference the High Court held that it fell within the mischief of section 10(2)(xi) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 as it had not been proved that the amount in question was a bad and doubtful debt in its money lending. On further appeal to this Court by special leave, HELD : The question whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Tribunal erred in disallowing a sum of Rs. 2,68,385/ written off by the appellant in their books of account as irrecoverable could be decided only after a supplementary statement of case was filed. [419 D] (i) The question should have been referred to the High court under section 66(1) of Income tax, 1922, which is a mixed question of law and facts. The question must be answered in the negative. It is true that the Tribunal after catalogueing the arguments advanced at the bar, has come to certain abrupt conclusions but all the tame it cannot be denied that the findings reached by the tribunal are findings of fact and those findings are supported by the evidence on record. [420 E F] (ii) The Tribunal has found that the monies sent by the asses see to the Bombay firm were not loans made to the assessee in the normal course of business nor in respect Of any other business of the appellant. This finding covers the entire amount sought to be deducted.

The petitioners were owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. The petitioners filed petitions before the High Court challenging the acquisition on the ground that the awards in these cases had not been made within two years of the notification making the declaration under section 4 of the Act. The High Court granted interim stay of further proceedings in respect of the acquisition of the said lands. In these appeals by special leave, it was contended for the petitioners that as the awards were not made within the stipulated time, they had no locus standi to file the writ petition and prayed for interim stay. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The fact of the stay orders was highly material in the determination of these Special Leave Petitions. [565E] 2. The facts of the case are highly material and it is beyond dispute that the fact of stay orders were highly material to show that the award in these matters had lapsed. That fact alone amounts to suppression of material facts. On this ground alone, the special leave petitions are liable to be rejected. [566F] 3. The question whether the awards have been made or not has to be decided by the High Courts only when the respondents appeared in response to the notice and filed their counter affidavit. In the instant case, the petitioners obtained an interim stay from this Court directing status quo with regard to the possession of the lands in question in Special Leave Petition No. 294 of 1985 preferred against the order of the Karnataka High Court dated August 14, 1984 with which we are not directly concerned. Whatever the ultimate effect of the order was highly important and there is no reference in the special Leave Petitions to any to the stay order and it would be beyond dispute if the respondents were appeared in reply to the notices and filed the counter affidavit.[565G H; 566A] 4. The contention that as awards in those cases have not been challenged before this Court and are directly concerned with the question raised and the non disclosure of the same certainly amounts to suppressed material facts, cannot be accepted. [567B C] 5. If he fails to do so and suppresses material facts his application is liable to he dismissed.

The appellant bank claimed that under cl. (ii) of the Sastry award the adjustment basic pay in respect of each workman should be fixed on January 1, 1962 and not on January l, 1959. The question was whether the adjustment amounted to a change necessitated by the fact that the Desai award did not separate sub cl. 2(a), (b) and (c). Held, that the adjustment in the Sastry Award as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal was inherent in the 1934 award that increments for 1951 and 1952 should be provided after adjustments have been made under sub cls. (a),(b) or (c) of el. (iv) of para 5. The effect of cl. 3(ii) is to be worked out as on January Ist 1, 1959, the two increments provided by that award would come to Rs. 119 and not Rs. 100. The appellant bank 's contention was that the words "subject to rules (i) to (iii) " in sub cls.(a), and (b), of cl.(iv) were wide enough to include all those thus arrived at under sub cl.(a). Held further, that in cl. 5(d) of Sastry award there is a reference to the basic pay on January I, 1959 and cl. 4(b)(c) being subject to cl. The adjustment in this Award as amended by the Sastry Act was inherent. In effect the two increment provided in sub cl (iv), namely, for the year 1951 and 1953 were not made a separate clause.

The appellant, a public limited company, was interested in a property known as the Hastings House Property and the land of the respondent company. The respondent company entered into an agreement with the Government of West Bengal for the construction of a Five Star Hotel on a plot of land. The terms of the lease were not to be altered by the Government but only to the extent that the lessee would continue to get the services and facilities in the existing structures until they were demolished or destroyed. The appellant company was granted a lease of five star hotel at the expense of the Zoo. The lease deed provided for the allotment of 200 acres of land for that purpose. The first respondent company, however, did not pay any rent to the Government. The question was whether the Government was entitled to give it a lease in respect of the said 5 acres of the land. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government had no intention to spare for the facilities which were till then being provided by the government and that the acquisition of the remaining land was not for the purpose of building the five star hotels. The High Court held that the government was perfectly bona fide in granting the lease to the Zoological Garden and that it was not possible to give a contract to the appellant to construct a new hotel on the land, that the State Government had not given any such permission and that there was no question of any interference with the construction. The appeal by special leave was against the High Court 's judgment. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Government was right in granting lease to five acres of a land to the Taj Group of Hotels for the construc tion of a five star Hotel. [260F] 2.1 The Government had made available to the court all the relevant documents so as to satisfy the Court about the propriety of its action. In this case, the Government did not act with probity in not inviting tenders at all and it was only on that basis that the appellant could have moved the Government or taken other steps for the execution of the five projects. [261F] 3.2 The question whether the government had acted with proba ble mind to give the land to a particular person by a procedure known to law such as acquisition or requisition, does not necessarily depend on the facts and circumstances of each case. It is necessary either to hold a public auction or to invite tenders at arm 's length with the Taj group of Hotels. The court cannot lightly assume that the action taken by the Govern ment is unreasonable or without public interest because, as in the present case, there were no such proposal. [262H; 263A] 3(i) It was not forgotten that if the land was to be allotted to the fiveoost of the four star hotels it would be a very difficult task for the people to walk in.

The assessee, a Hindu Undivided Family, had two branches in the State of Uttar Pradesh. The assessee was a partner in a firm dealing in money and was carrying on business as grain tillers. contractors and brick kiln owners. The firm was stated to be running an oil mill and carrying on the business of advancing money and taking money on loan when necessary. The Income Tax Officer, who had held that the assessee did not make valid gifts aggregating Rs.67,560 received by his sons and grand sons and therefore the amounts had been wrongly included in his net wealth by the Income Tax officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal held that there was no valid gift of Rs.1 lakh made by transfer from the assessee to his sons, and that the amount had been rightly included in the net wealth of the assessee. On reference, the High Court held that it was not open to the assessee 's father or firms or companies to make a valid gift if any of the properties passing on the death of the donor by reason of which he could make the gift by such book entries. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Court was in error in answering the question in favour of the revenue. [127E] The assessee had made a gift of certain existing movies from his account books for some years and were thereafter referred to as "unsecured loans". The assessee 'is the karta of a Hindu undivided family. On 20th November, 1956, the assessee purported to transfer Rs.50,000 from his accounts to his son. The transfer was effected by debiting the assessee "in his account" in the books of account and by crediting the account in the name of the donee. But in such cases merely books entries would not suffice. [128F G] Gopal Raj Swarup vs Commissioner of Income Tax, U.P., ; , referred to. The High court was in a position to consider the question whether there was a valid transfer or trust in respect of the said amounts and to determine whether the sum of Rs,50,00,000 could not be included in its property passing on death or the company or H.U.F. on the date of gift.

The Orissa Superior Judicial Service Rules, 1963 were framed by the High Court of Orissa under article 309 of the Constitution. The rules provided that "the High Court shall hold such posts for an executive post whether permanent or temporary". Rule 3(b) of the Rules provided that the High Courts shall hold those posts for more than three years and in no case shall suffer from any disability to which a person may be appointed by the Governor under article 233. The State Government was empowered to appoint the secretariat staff as District Judges or as Additional District Judges as the case may be, after they had held those posts. Rule 3 provided that on the expiry of three years the High Commissioner would hold office for an unduly long time and the services of any judicial officer shall not suffer by reason of a person having been appointed to a post. The High Court was of the opinion that the power to appoint a secretariat as well as the deputy law Secretary, who had no authority to act as law secretary, superintendent and legal remembrancer could be exercised only by the Chief Justice. The Government accordingly promulgated the Orissa Superior judicial Service Rules 1963. Rule 4 provided that every member of the service shall be appointed on his own request by the State Government. The appellant was a member of a Subordinate Judicial Service. He was posted as District and Sessions Judge, Ganjam Boudh, in the same month. On October 10, 1966 he was posted at the secret Secretariat for a period of three months. In the next year he was appointed as Deputy Secretary to the Government of Orissa. The Chief Justice of Orissa, who heard the matter, passed an order on October 10 1966, directing that the appellant be posted as a member sales tax tribunal on the post of the Registrar of the High court. On March 6, 1967, the High COurt held that the officers had no power to hold the posts in question and directed the Government to implement the transfers ordered by it. The government filed an appeal before this Court against the order of the Single Judge. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The power to transfer District Judges from one post to another was not a mere executive power but was subject to judicial review. [161F] (2) The word "control" found in article 235 includes disciplinary jurisdiction as well. The word control is of wide import and includes disciplinary powers, both administrative and judicial. It is not a profitable task to extract a sentence here and there from a judgment and order passed by the Orissa High Court. [162G H] (3) The Government has already implemented that part of the order as well, those officers are now functioning in the posts to which they were transferred. The learned Single Judge should have appreciated the anxiety of the respondent State that judicial officers should not be allowed to acquire vested interest in the secret Secretariat.

The appellant purchased a share out of joint land owned by his vendors. The mother State, the respondent No. 1 and the father of the vendor, filed a suit for partition of the pre emption in 1973 but it was dismissed on the ground that it infringed Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution. Thereafter, a host of writ petitions were filed in this Court challenging the constitutional validity of section 15(1)(a) of the Punjab Pre emption Act, 1913. The High Court allowed the petition holding that there was no infringement of Article 19(1) (f) of Constitution. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the suit land belonged to more than one co sharer and had not been sold jointly by all the co sharers, he as a co shar holder was entitled to claim the right of pre empture under clause (fourthly) of section15(1). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The purport of the Court 's decision in Attam Prakash 's case was to deny the right to those relative or relatives of the vendors who were specified in the erstwhile first three clauses of section fifteen(1), even if they happen to be co shar holders. [127F] 2. In the present case, the appellant seeks to exercise the right conferred on him by that provision. The Courts below have negatived this contention solely on the basis that if an outsider is introduced as a Co sharer in a property it will make common management extremely difficult and destroy the benefits of ownership in common. [128F] 3.

The appellants and the two sons of the original plaintiffs, who were the wives of the first respondent, filed a suit for title and injunction. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the sale deeds were subsequent to 21.8.1987 and that the alienees had become owners of the property and had even maintained that there had been improvements of the properties by the alienee. In appeal, the High Court held that once the Court was satisfied that there was a compromise it was for the court to record the same and no option lay before the Court to act otherwise. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellants have not lost interest in the property prior to the compromise and are not able to point out any justification as to why the compromise should not be acted upon and on the basis of it the litigation may not be disposed of. [541F] 2.1 In view of the fact that there is a dispute regarding payment and has been entered into by the father and his two sons, the alienors have become owners in possession of the suit property, the sale deed indicates that a sum of Rs. 1 lakh had been received earlier and a net amount of Rs 77,124 being the amount paid by the appellants before the registering authority. The alienees have made an attempt to hold out that there were agreements for sale prior to 21st August, 1987 to third parties. The alienations are for about a purported consideration of Rs 4 lakhs. The sale deeds indicate that a large sum of money had been receive earlier and the net amount was paid before the registration authority.

The workers of the appellant company, Baroda, were granted leave to appeal as provided by section 49 of the , in respect of sick leave. The workmen also filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the award of the Industrial Tribunal on the ground that the benefit of sick Leave to its workmen was not available to them because they had been given temporary exemption from the operation of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the workmen were entitled to 7 days ' sick leave with wages on pro duction of a medical certificate. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant companies that the benefits could not be granted to them as they had not been allowed to accumulate under the award. HELD: The scheme of the benefits admissible under the Act cannot be said to cover the work men 's demand for sick leave to the extent allowed by the Tribunal. Section 61 of the does not in fact deal with the question of sickness leave. [83F] The Act does not, however, provide for any leave to be granted on full emoluments during the period of workman 's physical incapacity to earn his normal wages because of his sickness. It is apparent that the scheme of benefits admissible to workmen under the , cannot be held to cover all contingencies of sickness and in any event the first two waiting days are not covered. [84G] The Tribunal was, therefore, justified in its view that the workman were entitled tO 7 days sick leave w.e.f. December 14, 1969.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1) of the , with a view to preventing him from acting in any manner prejudicial to the security of India and to the relations of India with the Portuguese Government. The grounds were served on him along with the order of detention. He challenged his detention by means of a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The grounds cannot be considered to be vague merely because they are open to the challenge to the validity of the detention order. [391 C] (ii)The right of the detenue to be furnished particulars is subject to the limitation under article 22(6) which implies the right to be supplied adequate particulars of the grounds of detention, to enable a proper representation being made. These rights involve corresponding obligations on the part of the detaining authority. It follows that both the obligation to furnish particulars and the duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against public interest are vested in the detaining authoritY. [390 E F] (iii)The question as to whether the grounds furnished in the writ petition were vague or not, is a circumstance which may well be taken into consideration in deciding whether the ground can be considered as vague. The requirement of section 10(1)(a) of COFEPOSA is that the detaining authorities must disclose facts considered prejudicial to public interest and an obligation to communicate such facts to the detenu. [389 E F; 390 A] (iv)The failure to furnish the particulars and to give particulars of any fact involved therein was a circumstance, which could not be taken as irrelevant for deciding whether or not the grounds could be considered. The failure to disclose the facts as well as the ambit of the non disclosure must be clearly communicated to the detenue at the time when the grounds are furnished. [388 C D] (v)The mere fact that the grounds were vague does not amount to denial of all particulars and leaving the grounds absolutely vague. All the contentions raised by the appellant in this Court were without substance. The order of the High court must be set aside and the writ application must be dismissed. [387 E F].

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre. He was attached with a charge sheet under r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954. The Chief of the army Staff found him guilty of gross misconduct. On April 9, 1958, he was convicted by the Summary Court under r., 14 of Defence Rules, 1955. The respondent filed an appeal to the Central Government which held that r.14 of the Defence Rules did not apply to the case and that r, 14 was ultra vires the . In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that : (i) the rule was ultra rites as the respondent had no case; (ii) the provisions of the Rules were ultra vires. HELD: The Army Rules are ultra vires and must be held to have been ultra vires, because there may be a valid rule where under subject to the other provisions of rules, the Central Govern ment has been given the power to dismiss or remove an officer without being tried by a Court Martial; (iii) the words "subject to the provisions Of this Act" occurring in section 19 make section 19 subject to section 45 and the Central Govt. has no case. The words " subject to such rules, ' occurring in s.19 make it clear that there may he a valid r. [450 A B] (iv) Rule 14 of Army Rules is not ultra vires as it was not ultra rites. It was therefore ultra vires section 45.

The respondent Municipality was constituted under the C.P. and Berar Panchayat Act, 1946. The appellant was deemed to be a Panchayat under the Act. On January 14, 1964, the respondent filed an application under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for issue of a writ quashing the resolution dated April 6, 1964 passed by the Standing Committee on April 6. 1964, rejecting the claim of the appellant that it was necessary for the Panchayat to have the octroi limits fixed with the approval of the Collector before levying octroi under r. 21 of the Rules. The High Court held that the Panchayat Samiti could not dismiss the appeal as being barred by limitation because r. 5 of the Fees Rules was ultra vires the powers of the rule making authority. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) Rule 5 of a. 22 of the Act does not require the Panchayat 's to fix the octroi limit in the resolution passed under r,3 and r. 53. The rules prescribe the procedure for levying tax or fee and are not confined to octroi duty only. Rule 7 which deals with tax on buildings and lands also prescribes that the panchayat shall follow the procedure prescribed in rr. 3 and 4 before levying a tax on building and land. [220 D E] (2) The Standing Committee was entitled to deal with the appeal on merits. The only point urged by the appellant was whether the Company brought tea into its octroi limits of the Panchayat for consumption, use or sale therein. As it did not do so, the Municipality could validly impose octroi duty from January 14 1964. [221 E F] (3) Rule 4 requires a notice stating two things; (1 ) selection of the tax and the rate at which it is to be levied; (2 ) the rate. But the learned counsel for the appellant contended that this was not done in accordance with r.21, and (3). The High court held that as r.5 applied to all appeals under section 124(5) of the the fixing of the commencement of the period of limitation as the date of publication of the notice under r.,4 for all appeals is arbitrary and destructive of the right of appeal. But this interpretation was not correct, because r, 5 applies only to two items; (i) selection of tax and (ii) the rate of duty at which the appellant had to use or sold the property for purposes of consumption, etc.

The appellants were prosecuted under section 31(1) read with section 33(1). The appellants contended that the conciliation proceedings could be prolonged only if they were closed and no useful purpose would be served by holding a further meeting. Held, that section 12 of the , contemplates that the report should be made and the proceedings closed within 14 days of the commencement of the conciliation proceeding or within such shorter period fixed by the appropriate Government. Colliery Mazdoor Congress, Asansol vs New Beerbhoom Coal Co., Ltd., (A.I.R. referred to. Held further, that the provisions of section 12(6) of the Act are applicable to all conciliation proceedings whether in regard to utility services or otherwise. The provisions of sub section 2 apply to all Conciliation Proceedings before a conciliation officer and not to pending proceedings. The object of conciliation is to get a settlement made with expedition and therefore under section 20(2)(b) of tile Act an application for reference must be made within 14th October, 1953, and the conciliation proceed ings were deemed to take place when the report was received by the Government. Workers of the Industry Colliery, Dhanbad vs Management of the industry Colliery, , referred to and distinguished. Workers ' of the respondent company, as also the appellant No. 1, were rightly convicted under section 3(1)(a) of that Act. Workers in the Industry colliery Colliery, could not be convicted under s.31(1), read with s.33(2) of Act.

The petitioner was detained under the provisions of the , by an order dated 2nd January, 1983 passed by the respondent No. 1 under section 3(2) of the . The grounds of detention were that on 24th December 1985 between 10th and 10th January 1986 the subject matter of the incident had been referred to a committee constituted for the purpose of enquiry into the exchange of fire between two rival groups. A criminal case was registered against the petitioner in respect of the exchange, of fire by the area where he was already in custody. The petitioner challenged his detention before the High Court on various grounds but the petition was dismissed without any speaking order. In this writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution it was contended that the order of preventive detention could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order was necessary for putting him back in jail, and that the service of the order had been properly made. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The grounds for forming the satisfaction for the need for the detention were there, and there was rational nexus between the object of the detention order as contemplated by the Act and the materials on record. [910C] 2. It is well settled in our constitutional framework that the power of directing preventive detention given to the appropriate authorities must be exercised in exceptional cases as contemplated under the various provisions of different statutes dealing with preventive detention and should be used with great deal of circumspection. There must be awareness of the facts necessitating preventive custody of a person for social defence. If a man is in custody and there is no imminent possibility of his being released, the power Of preventive detention should not be exercised. [936E F] 3. The order of detention though justified when it was passed but at the time of service of order there was no proper consideration of the fact that the detenu was in custody of that there was any real danger of his release. Nor did it appear that before the service there was consideration of this aspect properly. [810G] Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate, Burdwan & Anr., ; and Ramesh Yadav vs District Magis trate Etah & Ors., W.P. (Crl.) No. 2 96/86 dated 25th September, 1986, referred to.

The appellant company manufactures gold trade, i.e., manufacturers shroffs and dealers in gold. The respondents engaged the appellants to manufacture gold trade. The appellants were manufacturing gold trade and were selling it. The respondent company was also manufacturing gold. In the year of assessment the Income Tax Officer held that the appellants were guilty of gold trade under section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the order of the Income tax Officer. The High Court in revision set aside the order and declared sec. 28 of Act to be invalid. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the Administrator as well as the High Court had struck down section 28 in the manner done and in its view the license could not be granted or refused to grant permission. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The objective, the policy and scheme of the Act together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the , afford more than sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. [955E] Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias vs Asst. Collector of Central Excise, Poona, ; and Harak Chand Baksh Singh vs Assistant Collector of Customs, Central Excise Poona, II Division, ; , referred to. 2. The object of the enactment and the scheme affords sufficient guidance for the Administrator to grant or renew a license to a dealer. [953F] 3. In view of the fact that no express rule prescribing the conditions or circumstances under which the permission can be granted, or refusing to grant the permission should be exercised by the Administrator, the Administrator is not justified in striking down sec.28 of the . The objective is not to ensure the prevention of circumstances in making his orders. [951B] Harkchand Ratan Chand Banthria vs Union of India & Ors., ; , followed.

The appellants were the descendants of a deceased person. The property in dispute was granted to the respondents by the then manager of a Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments, who died in 1947. After the death of the said trustees, the respondents filed a suit for possession of the properties on the ground that they had been granted in Inam to the deity and its properties were alienated from time to time. The appellants contended that the lands were not granted to them as they belonged to the temple and that the respondents had acquired title by adverse possession. Held, that the appellants were entitled to the property. The right of the respondents to challenge the title of the appellants was not affected adversely if the alienation was made by the manager without his consent. The fact that the alienees had been removed from management of the temple de facto, did not affect the validity of the title. The question as to whether the alienee was entitled to a share in the property or a valuable consideration was irrelevant for the purpose of article 134 B. The respondents were entitled only to a declaration that they were entitled under the Inam to properties. The character of the representations made by them did not depend on the existence of any right to challenge an alienation made by their predecessor in title. Held further, that even assuming that the alienations were valid, the appellants had no right to resist the alienations. The suit was brought within article 134B and the respondents could not be allowed to challenge it after the expiry of 12 years from the date of the transfer. Held also, that as the alienors had been dispossessed by the predecessor in interest of the appellant 's father, the alienation made in favour of the deity was binding on the appellants. The title of a person who challenges an alienation is not lost by adverse posses sion and it is open to doubt whether such possession is adverse or not. Held therefore that the suit must be dismissed.

The respondent firm was dissolved in the year 1966 and its partners were dissolved. The appellant firm filed a suit against the respondent for dissolution of the cinema theatre on the ground that the cinema licence granted to it had been granted to Shri Ved Gupta, the proprietor of the firm, by virtue of the provisions of the Jammu & Kashmir Cinema (Regulation) Act, 1958 read with Rule 88(3)(a) of the Rules. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the license was granted in favour of Ved Gupta and not against any party other than the licensee. On appeal, the District Judge confirmed the order of the trial court. In the Letters Patent Appeal filed by the respondent, the High Court held that the licence granted in the name of Ved Order was a valid one and consequently the suit was maintainable. The High Court also dismissed the writ petition filed by M/s. Apsara Theatre. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1. The license granted in respect of the Apsar Theatre is not a licence in contravention of the law. [592 F] 2. The licence granted for the cinema was in favour by the proprietor who alone was the licensee and one of the partners obtained a licence from the licensing authority. No legal right or legitimate expectation of the Firm or its partners can be said to have been affected by the said order passed by the District Magistrate, for the simple reason that no person can be recognised as having a right to contravene the provisions Of the Act prohibiting exhibition of cinematograph films in public by any one other than a licensee or his authorised representative. [591 F] 3. The principle of natural justice is not attracted to such a situation and there was no obligation on the part of the District Magis trate to give a notice or hearing to the firm or its partner before he passed the impugned order. [593 C D] 4. The right to conduct the exhibition of the cinematograph films is conferred Cinema Theatre in the cinema by the Nagar Mahapalika, which is an essential element. It is not possible to uphold the view expressed in the judgment under appeal that "the licence granted" in the Gandhi Nagar Cinema is a grant for the premises and constitutes an interest attached to the premises. The order of license is one of mere partners obtaining a licence and one such partner becomes entitled to it necessarily follows the title in such building and the cinematograph". [593 F G] 5. The distinction between the cinema and the licensee is that the right to participate in the exhibition must be different from the owner or manager or partner of the licensed premises or a partner of a cinematography. The object and purpose of this section obviously is to empower the licensing authori ty to revoke the licence in the event of the commission of an offence under Section 6 or Section 6 E of the Act, not merely by the licensee but also by any person who may be in actual charge of a cinema. [595 F G; 593 A B] 6. The power to suspend a licence is conferred on the authority to revoke it upon such conditions in violation of the laws. The licensing authority has no jurisdiction to suspend the licence. [596 C D, E] 7. The question whether a license granted for a place of cinematograph without a licence can be revoked solely depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. A licence is liable to be revoked not merely when the licensee has been convicted of an offense under Section 3 or Section 4 but also in the absence of a licence. The principles of natural Justice are not attracted in such a case. [598 G H] 8. The word 'licence ' in the context of the section means a licence granted by the licensing on November 11, 1966 and it is clear that far from supporting the view taken by the Acting Chief Justice that the licensee had no right whatever to exhibit cinematograph films, there was nothing in law which would justify the licence taken out of the theatre without a license in contravention thereof.

The appellants were displaced persons and on 30 8 1952 the respondent entered into an agreement with them, for the purchase of the stock of raw materials, unsold finished goods, spare parts, cars etc. The appellants were also put in possession of the mills and the factory on 31 8 1952. On 12 2 1954 the respondent issued a notice to the appellants under section 7 of the , terminating their lease and called upon them to show cause why the lease should not be cancelled and why they should not been evicted. The notice was served on the appellants on 30 9 1952, but it was returned unserved as no notices were given by the appellants. On 13 2 1954, the respondent filed a suit for a declaration that the lease granted in favour of the appellants was void under section 12 of the . The appellants contended that section 12 was ultra vires the powers of the Custodian under section 10 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act and that the notice was ultra rites as it did not give any authority to issue the notice in question. Held, that the suit was barred by section 12 Of the , as it could be instituted only so as to override a bar imposed by any law but not the contract under which the lease was held and the appellants were entitled to have the same set on record. Aswini Kumar Ghosh vs Arabinda Bose, I.L.R. , referred to. The provisions of section 12 are not ultra vires and do not affect the power conferred upon the Custodian to cancel a lease granted by him.

The respondent father was a minor son of the appellant. The Sub Divisional Officer, Hanumangarh, by his order dated 10th August, 1972 determined the ceiling area for the appellant in respect of his father. The sub Divisional officer held that the father and son constituted two separate units and each one of them was entitled to get 62 Bighas and 16 Biswas as surplus land. It was further held that he was only 13 years of age when the ceiling proceedings were finalised by the Sub Divisional officer on 5th May, 1976. He therefore remanded the case to the Sub divisional Officer for fresh determination of the ceiling. The respondent 's application for adducing additional evidence in support of his contention was rejected by the sub divisional officer. On appeal, the Revenue Appellate Authority set aside the order of the Sub Divi sioner and remanded the matter to the sub Divisional Officer for re assessment of the land in question. In pursuance of the direction of the Board of Revenue, the Sub Division Officer held that there is no provision for separate units in Chapter III B of the Act of 1955. The Board went on to hold that there was no provision in Chapter Ill B of Act of 1956 for separate unit in Chapter 111 B of tho Act of1955 and dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the section confers executive powers of superintendence and control on the Board and it does not vest any power of superintendence on the board on judicial side. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'code ' in Section 221 of the Indian Act of 1954 is not subject to the other provisions of the , but only with respect to the Board constituted one unit and not two units and the case was remanded to Sub Divisional Offi cer, Hanumantha Rao for fresh deter mination of the calling area for Raghubir Singh. [726C D] 2. The power of general superintendence and Control over all revenue courts vested in the Board could not be exercised to the detriment of the writ petitioners much less by way of suo motu exercise of powers. [ 728D E] 3. Section 221 does not empower the Board to question any judgment of inferior court which was not otherwise subject to appeal or revision. Section 222 of the Code is similar to section 107 of the Government of India Act, 1915 and there is nothing illegal in it. The words 'codes in Chapter Il B of tile Act of 1953 for superintendence by the High Courts ' are consistently interpreted to mean that the High Court had power in appropriate cases to interfere with the judicial orders of the courts. [627E F] 4. Section 220 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 is not subjected to the provisions of section 221 of Government of lndia Act of 1935 in the Act. The High Court has by its order dated 14th April 1975 upheld the order passed by the Board. [ 728F G] 5. Section 218 of the Punjab Tenancy Act provides that the executive powers and control over all Revenue Courts vested in, the Board shall be subordinate to the Collector thereof. It does not confer any power on the Boards to set aside their orders of sub Divisional Officers provided it comes to the conclusion that interest of justice requires exercise of such powers. The Boards noticed that there were a gross and patent illegality in the order dated 15th August 1972 directed that the ceiling, area may be determined according to old law i.e. Act of 1960 and it spite of it the SubDivisional Officer committed the grave illegality on not merely ignoring the law but also ignoring the directions of the board of Revenue itself. The appeal consequently fails and is dismissed with costs.

The respondent, a journalist, was employed as a journalist and was published in the newspaper. The newspaper contained a number of advertisements issued by the company. The company filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the notice served on it by the Deputy Labour Commissioner, Nagpur, calling upon it to implement the orders of the Central Government made under section 12 of the Act. The High Court accepted the plea of the first respondent and declared that the law reports published by it were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2(b) of the and that the demand made by the State Government was unsustainable. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellant company it was contended that the Law reports published in respect of the past activities of the company should be construed as a newspaper and the employees engaged in their production or distribution were entitled to the benefit of the orders passed by the Central Govern ment on the basis of the recommendations made by it. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law reports which are being published by the Ist respondent are newspapers within its meaning. [785B] 2. The expression "newspaper" as defined in section 2 (b) includes not merely `public news ' but also `comments on public news '. Every law report contains the editorial note at the commencement of the decisions printed therein and also comments on some of the recent decisions. Law reports also contain, newly enacted Acts, rules and regulations, book reviews and advertisements relating to law books, handwriting and finger print experts etc. [783F] 3. The first respondent cannot derive any assistance from the deci sion of the High court in its judgment dated 22nd April, 1983. The second respondent cannot draw an adverse inference against the decil lating body for whose benefit the Act is passed has to be accepted. [784G] 4. The fact that a law report could be used as a reference book at later stage was not sufficient to hold that the laws report did not contain public news when it was received by the subscriber. [ 784A B] 5. The mere question whether a law reports can be published or not does not occupy a substantial part of a law Report to make it a newspaper, the publication of the last two years of the public are law reports to make them a newspaper. [781C D] 6.

The respondent landlord filed a ejectment proceeding against the appellant under section 41 of the . The appellant tenant resisted the eviction petition on the ground that he was a licensee and had been using the premises as such for the purpose of carrying out his business. The trial court passed a decree in ejectment petition holding that the respondent was a tenant within the meaning of section 15(2) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates and Lodging Houses Rates and Rent Act, 1947. The appellant filed an appeal before the High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution. The High Court allowed the revision petition on 9th December, 1975 holding that since the respondent had failed to prove that he had been a licensee, he was not entitled to terminate the tenancy earlier. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant tenant that (i) the application was not maintainable and (ii) the court of Small Causes had no jurisdiction to proceed with the application filed under section41 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The respondent landlord has been carrying on business for some time. It is a licence and not a lease. good deal of submission was made before the Court that if it was a lease and not licence then this point could be taken in aid of the submission that the court had jurisdiction to dispose of the application under section 40 of the. [1068C D] 2. The finding of the High court that the respond ent was in occupation of the premises under a subsisting licence was wholly wrong and suffered from serious infirmities of law and fact and deserved to be set aside. [ 1069E F] 3. In view of the legal position, the respondent landlord had not been able to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt amounting to almost an absurdity. It was a possible view. That is sufficient for this Court to uphold the finding of fact of the trial court or interfere under Article 226 of the Constitu tion over such decision. [1169F G] 4. The distinction between leave and licence has been well enunciated in Halsbury 's Laws of England, Fourth Edition, Volume 27 page 13. In determining whether an agreement creates a lease rather than a licence, the decisive consideration is the intention of the parties. [1106G H] 5. In the instant case, the appellant landlord had been carrying out business for sometime, and it was not a licensee. good dealing of the tenant under the Bombay Rent Act. The premises in question were leased to the respondent under a licence granted by the Court of Small Cause Court. The lease was executed and was renewed on 31st March 1966. Thereafter, the owner of the suit premises filed an ejectment proceeding under section 42 of the , against the respondent. The Trial Court passed a simple decree for eviction against the tenant. The appeal preferred by the respondent before the District Judge was allowed and the order of the Court was affirmed.

The respondent was a Ruler of the former Jodhpur State. He was governed by the United State of Rajasthan which formed part of the erstwhile State of Udaipur. The United State was formed in 1948 and became Part B State of Jaipur. In 1947, the United States of Rajasthan merged with the United state of Rajasthan. On the merger of the United states of Rajasthan, the former State of Dholpur became the Part B States of Jaipur and the United Sthan Government became the part of that State. The new State was a sovereign and was governed in 1949 by the Covenant entered into by it with the Dominion of India after August 20, 1947. In 1948, the respondent applied to the District Court for refund of the amount paid as export duty in advance under the agreement dated January 26, 1950. The District Judge held that the liability of the State of Bikaner to refund was not fasten on the State and that the State had been bound by the obligation of the new sovereign to pay the export duty. On appeal, the District judge held that (1) the liability was not extinguished under article 295(2) of the Constitution; (2) the agreement was a valid one and (3) the respondent was liable under article 296(2).
