The High Court on reference, however, held that as the United Provinces of Rajasthan had been merged into the United Dominion of Rajasthan on January 26. 1950, the liability to refund could be met only by the respondent under article 294(2), but this decision was reversed in appeal by the State. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1)(a) The new sovereign throughout India continued all the old laws till they were altered or repealed and there was specific provision in each Covenant that the assets and liabilities of the Covenanting States would continue and assume all liabilities arising from the existence of those laws. Otherwise it follows that there was always recognition by the new State of its liability in the manner already referred to with respect to the liabilities of its merging States, and if there was any doubt about it that doubt in our opinion is resolved by the existence Of article VI or similar provision throughout the process of these political changes. [182 B C] (b) The agreement between the Ruler of Udaipur and the appellant could not be said to have been recognised by the Government of the States because there was recognition of liability even on the principles enunciated in Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd. vs State of Ajmer, ; , that the new state recognised the rights of the subjects and undertaken the liability, if any arising against the merging State. [183 E] (c) The appellant could derive no assistance from the case of Maharaja Shree Umaid Mills(1), because, in view of article 295 of the Consti tution it was not permissible to contend that the expression "Government of the corresponding Indian State" used in article 295 must mean only the United Government as it was on January 27, 1950 or would also include all the former States which came to be merged into it through the process to which we have already referred. [184 E F] (d) The liability lay upon the State under article I36 of the covenanting State throughout this process and under the circumstances the suit was main tainable against the Part C State of Jodhpur in view Of article 295. [185 G] (e) The contention that the agreement between Ruler of Rajasthan and the former Ruler of Jodhpur was binding on the Part D States must fail. Article VI of the Agreement provided that the liabilities and liabilities arising out of any contract or otherwise shall be the assets of the Union, the new States being to continue till they are repealed or altered by the New State. Therefore, under article VI of a Covenant the liability lay on the appellant and not on the part B State which had merged into United State before the Constitution came into force.

The appellant company was a dealer in cotton and groundnut. The State Government issued a notification under section 5(1) of the Madras Commercial Crops Markets Act, 1933, directing the establishment of a market committee at the place of a Market for the purchase and sale of commercial crops in the State of Madras. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification by filing writ petitions before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the applications. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the provisions of section 5 were not only unreasonable but also violative of article 19(1)(f) and (g); (ii) the notification did not provide for any reasonable restriction on the appellants ' right to do business; (iii) the notifications were ultra vires as they infringed articles 14, 19(6), 31(2) and 31(3); (iv) the Act was void because it imposed unreasonable restrictions on the petitioners ' fundamental rights under article 19 (1)(g); and (v) the impugned provisions of the Act constituted reasonable restrictions on a citizen 's right to carry on any profession or business. HELD: (i). The notification did provide for the imposition of the market fee and was therefore invalid. [108 B] (ii). The object of the impugned sections is to protect the producers of commercial crop from being exploited by them. The provisions of sections 5(2), 5(3) and 6 of the , are not only reasonable restrictions but also tend to defeat the very purpose of the legislation. Therefore, having regard to the entire scheme of the . Act, the impugned section does not offend article 19. [109 C] (iii). The question whether a particular payment is a trade allowance or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [110 D E] (iv). The provisions in sections 5 and 6 do not contravene articles 14 and 19(i)(f), 31 and 31 (3) of State Act, as they are only consequential to the object of section 15 of the Central Act. [111 F G] (v). The scheme of a statute is to provide for a reasonable restriction of the trade in the commercial crops and the market to be built up and given or transferred, it would not be a trade allowances for the purpose of this Act. A market committee generally may make bye laws for the regulation of the business and conditions of trading therein and particularly it can make bye law prescribing what are permissible trade allowances under the section. Such allowances as are prescribed by a bye law can be deducted in any transaction notwithstanding the fact that they are trade allowances. The object is to safeguard the growers, the producers, the traders and the sellers, the producer, the commodity sold and the price paid for the sale. Allowance means something given as compensation, rebate or deduction. [112 F G; 113 A B] In the present case, the appellant company had a large trader with the State Government and it was not possible to pay any fee on the price or commodity within the meaning of section 14 of the and therefore, they could not be called 'any trade allowance '. [114 E] The provisions relating to the levy of market fees were not so wide as to enable the Government to supersede them. [115 G] In any event, the Act did not contravene article 19 of the Constitution. [116 A B]. (ii)(a) The object was to protect producers, producers and producers from being allowed to trade in and about the place where market is fixed, and other relevant considerations which cannot now be visualized. [117 C] In this case, there was no material on record to arrive at a definite finding that the appellant 's trade was only an incident of ownership of the property. The Act did provide that the trader was entitled to carry out his business in the market established subject to the regulations and also provided for certain other places and only small amounts were to be paid for every additional premises for the same purpose.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed his conviction but reduced the sentence to transportation for life. The appellant contended that the sentence should be reduced to transportation in view of the fact that he had been acquitted by the Sessions Judge, because (1) the evidence against him was not corroborated by any previous arrangement; (2) the conviction could not be sustained on that basis as it was based on circumstantial evidence and (3) the appellant must have been convicted under s.302 of the Penal Code for murder. Held, that the High Court erred in its view that the death sentence should have been reduced to life imprisonment. The circumstances relied upon by the prosecution were : (1 ) that the deceased was a tenant of the appellant; (ii) that the appellant was guilty of the offence under section 326 of the Code and (iii) that he was liable for the murder. The fact that the accused was acquitted did not mean that the conviction must be maintained but only that it could be altered to transportation. Mamand vs Emperor, (1924) L.R. 52 I.A. 40, referred to. In the present case there was no evidence of prior meeting of minds to form a pre arranged plan because the appellant had been convicted by the High court and his conviction under section 307 was not justified. The facts disclosed do not warrant an inference of common intention in the present ease. The sentence should therefore be reduced. Mamad vs Emperor (1923) L,R. 51 I. A. 40 and Mahbub Shah vs King Emperor (A.I.R 1946 P.C.

The petitioner was a Sub Divisional Engineer in the Central Public Works Department. He was compulsorily retired by an order dated 3.8.1976 with effect from 5.11.76 made under Rule 56(j)(i) of Fundamental Rules. The petitioner challenged the said order before the High Court on the ground that he was holding an officiating appointment in Class II service and was not entitled to draw up a fresh date of superannuation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the petitioner that as the petitioner was holding a substantive appointment in class II service he could not have been compulsorily retired under sub clause (i). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. Rule 56 (j) of the Fundamental Rules is meant to cover only those who are in a post on a regular basis, i.e., in a substantive basis, and not on an officiating basis only. [637C] 2. Sub clause (ii) does not apply to the facts of this case as the peti tioner had not attained the age of 55 years by the date of the order. The observations made in Tahilia ni 's case clearly support the petitioner. But the correct ness thereof is disputed by the counsel for the Union of India and that is why the Court has given effect to the decisions of the Delhi High Court. [ 634D E] 3. Sub Clause (ii), is the general rule applicable to all Government servants and sub clause(i) carves out a class of Government servants into a category and makes a special provision. The purpose of Fundamental Rule 56 is to confer power on the appropriate authority to compulsorily retire government servant in the public interest and the classification of Government serv ices into two categories covered by sub clauses (i) and (ii). [638E F] 4. Sub cl.(i) doesnot apply to Government servants in Class I or Class II Service or post on substantive, temporary or offi ciating basis. On this conclusion the writ peti tion is liable to be dismissed. [737F G] 5.

The respondent, a husband of the appellant, died intestate on 12.1.1961. He had filed a suit against his wife and children for recovery of Rs. 50,000/ as damages from the appellant. The trial court held that there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation. On appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment and decree of the trial court holding that there Was no concluded insurance contract between deceased and his wife. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the deceased was the only authority to accept the proposal; (ii) the letter and the letter were not signed by the deceased after the death of the Corporation; and (iii) in any event, the Corporation must be deemed to have waived by its conduct the formality if any, of sending communication of its acceptance to the person if all the formalities were not complied with. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in appreciating the facts and evidence in this case. When an insurance policy becomes effective is well settled by the authorities but before we note the said authorities it may be stated that it is clear that the expression "underwrite" signifies accept liability under '. The dictionary meaning also indicates that. (i). In the instant case, there was a general statement that there were no con tempt or averment that the Divisional Manager had accepted the proposal on the contrary he his deposition as an officer of the corporation. [358F G] 2. The mere receipt and retention of premium until after the deceased had died, does not mean consent and no binding contract arises until the person to whom an offer is made says or does something to signify his acceptance. Mere delay in giving an answer cannot be construed as an acceptance. Acceptance must be signified by some act or acts agreed on by the parties or from which the law raises a presumption of acceptance.

The appellants applied for an interim injunction restraining the Bank of India from taking any steps in pursuance of a letter of credit opened in favour of M/s. V.V. D.K. Cassim & Sons, which was the subject matter of the suit. The trial court granted an interim order restraining the bank from taking proceedings in pursuance thereof and remanded the suit for trial. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order of the High Court amounted to a judgment or a decree and the expression "final order" in section 205(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935, meant a final decision on the rights of the parties in dispute in a suit or proceeding; and that the expression 'final order ' in section 109 Code of Civil Procedure means an interlocutory order passed by the Court of the rights and obligations of the party in dispute. HELD: The order refusing to grant interim injunction did not determine the rights, and obligations, of the respondents in relation to the matter in dispute, in the suit or proceedings from which appeal has arisen, was not final within the meaning of article 133(1)(a) and (b). [707 D] In the present case the order refusing an interim relief did not finally dispose of a suit. It was not a final order within the contemplation of article133(1), because, the plaintiff 's suit as a result of the order was disposed of by the order directing the filing of a complaint under section 205 read with section 114 I.P.C. [708 G H] Mohanlal Maganlal Thakkar vs State of Gujarat, ; and Mohanlal Magan Lal Thakkar vs The King, , referred to.

The respondent assessee, a manufacturer of cotton fabrics, was selling the goods manufactured by it and the process of manufacturing was done through its factory gate. The factory gate in question means the "deemed" factory as if the processed fabric was sold by the processor. In order to explain the position it is made clear by the following illustration: If the trader who entrusts cotton or man made fabric to the processor for processing on job work basis, would give a declaration to the manufacturer as to what would be the price at which he would be selling the processed goods in the market, that would be taken by the Excise authorities as the assessable value of the processed fabrics and excise duty would be charged to the fabric on that basis provided that the declaration as to the price of the grey cloth in the hands of the processor plus manufacturing profit and manufacturing expenses, but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. The respondent assessee claimed that the assessablevalue of the processing should be the value of grey cloth and excise duties would be paid to the processed manufac turing cotton fabric. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim on the ground that the valuation was not at which it was selling its fabrics, but only the price or deemed price at the factory gate for the processed cloth. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal held that the value could be the basis of the assessable market and that the assess ment should be determined on the basis that the price paid would be a price at where the assessable goods were sold in the open market. The High Court also rejected the reference made to it. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The assessable value is the value for the grey fabric or fabric plus the value thereof which will either be included in the price charged by the processing manufa turing the process basis, plus manufacturing profits and the manufacturing expenses but not the other subsequent profits or expenses.[345C] 1.2 In order that the market value of processed fabric would be determined with the assessable valuation of the cloth and the person so authorised agrees to discharge all the liabili ty under the said Act and the rules made thereunder, it is necessary to include the processor 's expenses, costs and charges plus profit, but it is not necessary to included the trader 's profits who gets the fabrics processed, because those would be post manufacturing profits. [345E] 1:3 The price at Which he is selling the cloth must be the valuation of grey fabric and excise Duty would be chargeable to the processing charges on that footing provided that it would be calculated in accordance with the provisions of the Act. [346F] 2.1 If the traders who entrustles cotton or manufacture to theprocess work basis the value would be Rs.30, being included in price at a factory gate or deemed to be the prices at the Factory gate for processing. The price of grey fabrics plus the cost of the job work done plus manufacturing expenses and themanufacturing expenses but cannot be included as the trader "s profits" who gets them processed because those will be postmanufacturing profits. It is necessary that the trader, who entrustts cotton or manufactured fabric to him for processing, should discharge all these liabil ities under the Act and rules made there thereunder. [347G H] 2:2 If the assessee who entrust sits cotton or january to the job worker for processing at a fabric, he would give the declaration to him as to how would be price at what he would he selling the processing goods in that market, and would be taking by the excise authorities as his assessable value. [349A] 2 :3 If the dealer who entrust ing cotton or manufacturer made fabric is required relating to the prices of grey yarn plus manufacturing cost and manufacturing expense but not no other subsequent loss or expenses, it would he necessary to including the trader in getting the fabrics processing, because these would be Post manufacturing profits, and the manufactured goods plus the manufacturing profit.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963. He was confirmed in that post in course of time. On January 21, 1974 he was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis. On March 14, 1975 the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act 1973 introduced extensive amendments in the Act of 1961. Section 33 of the Amending Act provided for appointment to the Panchayats. The appellant was confirmed with effect from April 1, 1975. He filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the High court on the ground that he had been appointed as an Assistant Secretary on March 14.1975 and was confirmed later on. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that by reason of section 14(4) of the amending Act, the Panchayat Samiti lost its power to make appointments to the Panchayat. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appointment of the appel lant to the post of a Head clerk in any event was not made after June 13, 1973 when the Amending act came into force. There is no substance in this contention. Even assuming for the purposes of argument that the right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant was entitled to be consid ered as a head Clerk on the date on which it purported to do so. Clearly, it had fortified that right on June 13. 1973. It could not, therefore, have appointed the appellant as a Subordi nate clerk in the Panchayat Samities. He is appointed lawfully to the posts of a clerk and that is the post in which the Government has absorbed him. [737F H] 2. The fact that the appellant is promoted as Head Clerk in January 1974 or the further fact that he was appointed on April 1. 1975 cannot improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after July 13,1973 when the amending act came to force.

The appellant, a Mahant of Math Sauna, was in possession of the property in dispute as Mahant and Sarbarakar. The property included properties in village Amauli. He asserted that he was in posses sion of the Math Saunti and was therefore entitled as Sarbarkar Mohant Shivshankar Yati. He further claimed a finding that the income from the properties belonged to the Math and not to the institution or the temple or the deity. The trial court decreed the suit but included a finding in his judgment that Sadashiv Yati was not a regularly constituted Mahant of the deity, and that he had been in possession thereof as Mahant. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court allowed both the appeals and set aside the decree of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that: (1) The fund from which the Amauli properties were acquired constituted the personal property of Mahant Shivshanker Yati; (2) the Amara nee was holding in high regard on account of his personal learning and attainments, and had a large number of chelas including many affluent persons from whom he received personal bhents or pranamis of large amounts of money. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The fund could not be said to belong to the math or the appellant 's Hindu Law of Religious and Charitable Trusts. [663 H] 2. In the present case, it is difficult to conclude from the material before the Court that the total income from properties belonging to the respondent Math and the deity left any appreciable surplus after meeting the expenditure on account thereof. The High Court was right in holding that the Amaati property constituted the respondent 's personal property. [665 B C] 3. In view of the fact that the fund from where the Ama corpus was acquired constituted, the income could not form part of the properties of the math Sauna or of the appellant deity Sri Thakur Gokarneshwar Mahadeoji. [664 D E] 4.

The appellants were displaced persons from West Pakistan. The Custodian of Evacuee Property, Punjab, cancelled the allotment of certain lands in favour of the appellants on the ground that they had been allotted to them under the notification issued by the Government of Punjab under section 12(1) of the East Punjab Evacuees and Land Reforms Act, 1954. The appellants moved the Deputy Custodian General for revision but the same was rejected. On appeal the Additional Custodian held that the allotment in favour was not a result of misapprehension of the actual facts and that they were not entitled to allotment of suburban property under section 19 of the Act. The order was confirmed by the Custodian General on appeal. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The power conferred by section 19(1), of the , is to prevail notwithstanding anything contained in any other law for the time being in force. Therefore, they must prevail over the provisions of section 19. [334 B] (ii) Section 10 of the 1954 Act does not help the appellants because there is nothing on record to show that a managing officer was appointed with respect to evacuee property acquired under the Notification dated March 24, 1955. The only effect of r. 102 is to permit cancellation of an allotment for reasons stated. That is all. [333 E F] Bal Mukund vs State of Punjab, ; , followed. The State Public Service Commission issued a notification inviting applications from eligible candidates for the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women) District Sonebhadra, Uttar Pradesh. The advertisement was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examination was over, the respondents were selected and appointed as Upper Zila basic Shiksha Adhikari. The recruitment process was completed on the basis of the results thereof. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the selection of the respondents for re holding the post. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 When no defect was pointed out in regard to the written test and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the written exami nation, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examination. On the other hand, the situation could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the ground of the written examina tion and select those who on the date of the selection process became eligible for selection. [125B C] 1.2 The situation could not have been suitably met by set aside the appointment and asking the High Courts to re hold the recruitment test. On account of improper feeding into the comput er some of the candidates who had better performance in the viva voce were not called and candidates securing lesser marks in the selection to litigation. [ 125E F] 1:3 The situation can have been properly met by putting aside the recruit ment and asking a fresh examination of all qualified candidates on account of the improper feeding to what has once been done and the litigation could have be avoided.

The appellant filed a suit against the respondent, his father and for impleading him. The suit was decreed on the allegation that there was one Shiromani Nirankari Dera at Patiala in Moga Tehsil and that he as mahant of the Gurdwara had the right to manage the properties attached to it. The prayer in the plaint was for recovery of possession of the Dera and the properties, attached to the Dwara. The appellant pleaded that the Dami could not recover possession of Dera because its lawful appointment was not binding on him. He also alleged that he was in possession of certain branches one at Landeke in Mog. The trial court decreed the suit. In second appeal the High Court held that after the death of Som Dass, the appellant was bound to bring on record his legal representatives within the period prescribed by law and that there had been no justification for setting aside the abatement. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) It is well settled that a succeeding trustee of a trustee who filed a claim as a mahant is entitled to manage his interest with the leave of the Court. When a suit is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of the interest of the representative, the rule that has to be applied is Order 22, Rule 10 of the Civil Procedure Code. [490 B C] (2) The word 'interest ' which is mentioned in this rule means interest in the property i.e., the subject matter of the suit and the interest is the interest in property i,e.,, the subject mater of the Suit. It is not confined to devolution of interest of a party by death, it also applies if the head of the mutt or manager of the temple resigns his office or is removed from office. In such a case the successor to the head 'of the mutta can be substituted as a party under this rule. [489 C D] (3) The suit against Som Dass was for possession and management of the dera and was decreed by the trial court. The High Court, in appeal, reversed the decree of the court below and held that the appeal had abated and dismissed the suit on merits.

The Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board, Andhra Pradesh, issued a notification dated January 1, 1983 under the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution fixing the age of retirement of all employees of the Andhra Pradesh Civil Service. The said notification was challenged by some of the employees of Andhra Pradesh in a writ petition before the High Court. A Division Bench of the High court allowed the writ petitions and quashed the notification dated February 8, 1983. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the proviso which conferred a benefit upon Government servants by protecting their conditions of service, cannot be struck down as invalid merely because they had not attained the age prescribed by the rules; that the power of a Commission to enquire into a question must depend upon the terms of the reference and not upon the statements made on the floor of the House. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The proviso to Rule 2(b) which conferred the benefit upon government servants by providing for an age of superannuation at 55 years does not violate article 14 or Article 16 since it is not arbitrary or unreasonable in the circumstances of the case. [605 B] 2.1 The power to enquire under rule 2(a) is political and is subject to judicial review. It is well settled that Article 311 (2) is attracted only when a civil servant is reduced in rank, dismissed or removed from service by way of penalty, that is to say, when the effect of the order passed against him in this behalf is to visit him with evil consequences. [505 E F] 2:2 The power conferred by Rule 2 (b) is not violative of Article 14 or article 16 since the rule making authority has no power to make rules for reducing the age. The power is plenary within its field like the power under the Proviso to Article 311(2). The power of the State Legislature to pass laws and there are no limitations upon that power except those to which the legislative power of State Legislature is subject. [065 F G] 2 :3 The power given by Rule 1 (b), in the instant case, is political in character and is to be distinguished from an ordinary rule making power. The Government has a discretion in the executive to pass the law regulating the age, but it cannot do so under the provisos to Article 162 of the Constitu tion. [075 G H] 2 .4 The power under Rule 2 is political. It does not fall within the powers of the rule made by the proviso. The rules and amendments made thereunder are issued by the State Government under the powers delegated to it by the Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1930. [085 A B] 3.1 In the instant cases, the power conferred on the State Legislatures by Rule 4 was political in nature within the field demarcated by the Constitution and it includes the power to legislate retrospectively. Therefore, the amendment made to the Fundamental Rules in the exercise of power conferred under Article 309 cannot be declared invalid for the reason of non application of mind, any more than any other law can be. [095 C D] 3:2. The amendment made by Rule 3 was not violative or employment of the conditions of serv ice and officers of the Court. It was not arbitrary nor unreasonable in that it was made under the said rule.

The Haryana General Sales Tax Act, 1948 was enacted to provide for the levy of purchase tax on raw materials in the State. Section 9(1) provides that no dealer shall be entitled to claim exemption from assessment, re assess ment or collection of any amount by way of tax made or purporting to have been made and any action taken or anything done under the provisions of section 9(2) shall, for all purposes be deemed to be and to have always been done or taken in accordance with law. Section 5(1)(b) provides for exemption only from tax on goods specified in Schedule B and not from sales which are specified in schedule B. The proviso thereto provides that the exemption under section 9 shall not apply to any goods other than those specified in Sch. B, Part C (ii). The proviso to clause (a) of sub section (1) of section 5 provides that where a dealer is required to pay tax outside the State in respect of any goods specified therein, he shall be liable to pay the tax sought to be levied on the purchase value of such goods at the rate notified under section 15(3). The appellant who was a registered dealer under the Central Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1976, filed returns for the assessment year immediately after the expiry of the period of exemption. The assessing authority rejected the assessee 's claim and the appellate authority held that the movement of goods outside India was occasioned by the contract between the S.T.C. and the foreign buyer and not by that between the appellant and the S,T.E. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the effect of section 6(a) was to expand the scope of section S so as to include within the concept of sales in the course of export outside India also the 'penultimate sales ' dealt with in the case of a dealer who purchased goods from the assessee and (ii) the sales made by him were not sales in 'the course of ' export outside the territory of India within the meaning of section 2(c)(i) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in concluding that the appellant was not entitled to the exemption claimed under section 24(1). [362C] 2. (a). The expression 'sale by him in section 9 (1), has to be given full meaning and in other words, the exemption is only to export goods specified as a whole of the turnover. [362D] 3. (b) The word 'turnover ' means the taking out of the goods from one part of 'taxable turnover '. The expression takes within its ambit all transactions which would not otherwise have come within the purview of section 4(1), and, therefore, section 6 will not come to the aid of the Revenue to support the levy. [363E] (c) The words 'for the purpose of section 8(1 )(b), ' in the raw materials purchased for manufacture of goods which are 'specified in Schedule C, State ' have to be read as 'provided ' in sub section 3 of section 10 of the Central Act. [364F G] (d) The expression "sale by himself" refers again to sale and purchase of goods specified under section 8. [365G H] (e) The appellant is not entitled either to exemption under s 24(2)(b). [366A B] (f) The High Courts in Haryana and Haryana have held that sales made in the instant case are 'penalties ' within the definition of 'turnover" as defined in section 2 (c)(ii) of Act.

The appellant firm was registered under the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1948. The goods were sent to the sellers on board and they were delivered to them by the sellers at some point of time after they had crossed the customs barrier. The sellers returned the goods to the buyers on September 30, 1956. The purchasers applied for exemption from sales tax in respect of the sales of cotton made by them but the sellers refused the request. The appellant 's contention was that the goods remained their property till these crossed the Customs barrier and thus entered the export stream and so no tax was realisable on these sales in view of section 10(b) of the Bombay Act. Held, that the words " a person " in section 8(b), as a registered dealer " in the context of the Export Control Order 1954, mean " the goods" used in the Act and not the goods which were exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b). The words " the time of export " in entry 5(2) of List II of VII Schedule to the Constitution are wide enough to include a registered dealers. Brandt 's case (supra) and Brandt vs 'M/s. Daulatram Rameshwarlal, , referred to. Held further, that when goods were imported into India by land, it was not necessary for the appellant to obtain the necessary export licence under article 19(1) (b) Of the Constitution. The words used in entry No. 5(1), as they stood before the amendment of the Import & Export Control Act, 1947, showed that the time when the goods went out of the territorial limits of India was within the meaning of the Imports and Exports Control Order, 1954.

The respondent husband married the appellant 's wife as a second wife. The initial warmth vanished and the jealousies of a triangular situation erupted marring mutual affection. The respondent divorced the appellant around July 1962. A suit relating to a flat in which the husband had housed the wife resulted in a consent decree which also settled the marital disputes. For instance, it recited that this respondent was still a wife while the respondent rejected this status and asserted that she was a divorcee. The trial court held that the appellant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ for the son and Rs. 400/ for her mother. On appeal by the aggrieved husband, the High Court confirmed the order of the trial court. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the courts below had ignored the plain provision in the Explanation to section 125(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure which provides that wife 's marriage is not a divorce; and (ii) that there must be proof of neglect to maintain to attract s.125 and his third contention was based on contractual arrangement in the consent decree read with section 127(3)(b). HELD: The High Court had not spoken at all. Moreover, the husband has not examined himself to prove that he has been giving allowances to the divorced wife. His case on the contrary is that she has forfeited her claim because of divorce and the consent order. Obviously, he has no case of non neglect. His plea is his right to ignore. So the basic condition of neglect must be made out if the hurdle of section 125 (4) is to be over come. [79 C D] The compulsive conclusion from a divorce by a husband and his provision of a separate residence as evidenced by the consent, decree fills the bill. Do divorcees have to 1) prove mutual consent to live apart? Divorce painfully implies that the husband orders her out of the conjugal home. If law has nexus with life this argument is still born. The last defence based on mehar payment, merits more serious attention.

The Collector of the district after considering the appellant 's representation dated 25th March, 1988 that there was no requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice had passed an order on 25th April, 1988 under which he placed in the black list for future under the orders passed by the Collector. The said order was challenged before the High Court by way of a writ petition. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the appellant was not required to be given notice and opportunity of making representation against the proposal of black listing. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The black listing any person in respect of business ventures has civil consequence for the future business of the person concerned in any event. Even if the rules do not express so, it is an elementary principle of natural justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. In that view of the matter, the last portion of the order in so far as it directs black listing of the appellant in respect to future contracts cannot be sustained in law. [868C D] 1.2 The High court was not justified in taking a different view of Rule of law that any order having civil consequence should be passed only after following the principles of natural Justice. It has to be realised that black listing no person in regard to business vvisors has civil consequences for the past business of a person concerned, in any case. Even assuming that the rules did not express any so, the High court is not justified on the basis of the view taken by the High Courts. [886D E] 1:3 The order directing black listing the appellant as per the order passed by Collector is set aside.

The appellant was the landlord of a property in Madras. The respondent filed a suit for possession of the property on the ground that the appellant had been using it as a shop and that the tenancy was based on the lease deed dated 30th July, 1947. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the building was not a 'land ' within the meaning of section 4(1)(b) of the Madras City Tenants Protection Act, 1949, but that the respondent had no right to evict the appellant because the property was not 'landless ' and that it was not open to the appellant to contend that the order of eviction was ultra vires. The appellate court affirmed the decision of the trial court. On further appeal, the High Court held that the lease was a sale of land and that therefore the respondent could not maintain the suit for recovery of rent based on section 11(2)(vii) of Act. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) since the lease granted by the lessor in favour of one of the tenants was invalid, the tenant had no title to the building standing on the site in question and (2) since a suit was filed for declaration that the said order of the Rent Controller was ultra rites, the respondent should have sought eviction. HELD: (1)(a) The lease granted to the lessee by the landlord was valid. [567 D] (b) The expression 'landowner ' in section 3(4) of that Act includes a Court of Small Causes disposing of an appeal from his order and it is not possible to escape the conclusion that the jurisdiction to be exercised by him is a limited one. It will be anomalous to hold that where an owner files a suit on behalf and other is entitled to recover the rents of the building which has been let out or would be entitled to receive rent of the buildings if it were let out to a tenant, in one of several capacities, the Rent Control Court may have to go into the tenant 's contentions on the issue but he is not to decide the question finally. [568 G H] (c) The jurisdiction of the Civil Court is excluded by section 4 from consideration only where the suit is instituted for arrears of rent and not for eviction. Therefore, the jurisdiction of a civil court is excluded. [569 B C] (d) The High Court was right in holding that it could not have invoked the general principles of res judicata. [570 G] (e) The decision of this Court in the earlier case was not final on the question whether the order in the present case was to be treated as an order of a court of competent jurisdiction. If the civil court had no jurisdiction to entertain an application except by a landlord or a tenant it would have been open to him to seek eviction by having his title adjudicated upon in a civil Court but that is not one of such direct issues. [571 G H; 571 A] (f) The question whether a suit or not was maintainable depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. If there is any dispute which arises between the parties as to whether the application falls within the jurisdiction under section 11, it is the Civil court which is competent to decide that dispute. [572 C D] In the present ease, the appellant 's suit was not one for a declaration of title and the High court erred in applying the statutory provisions of section 11 of the Act. The High court overlooked the fact that the application for eviction was made under section 4 of the Tamil Nadu City Tenants ' Protection Act.

The Mysore State Civil Service Association, respondent in the appeal, was a member of the Andhra Pradesh State Civil Services. He was given due opportunity to object to the proposed assign ment of a place to him in the seniority list. The appellant challenged the validity of the impugned order on the ground that the combined final gradation list dated April 6, 1962, so far as category 6 was concerned, was ultra vires and illegal and that it was not open to the respondent to make a representation with regard to the preliminary provisional inter State Seniority List although he was given opportunity to be heard. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant 's petition was premature as the final list of officers on an integrated seniority list was still to be prepared after hearing objections. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The combined final list dated 4th April 1962, is ultra vires, and illegal. [828 D] Shankariah 's case, ; , followed. (2) No element of punishment at all is involved in preparing either a provisional or a final seniority list, and all that is done is that certain principles are applied in the preparation of the list. These principles are generally found in the rules or executive directions which are known to or are capable of being found out by the persons affected. When a provisional seniority fist is prepared there is a possibility of some mistakes occurring about the facts of a case or in the application of those rules. It would, therefore, be quite fair to give a person affected an opportunity to he heard against the proposed fist before it is finalised so that any possible mistakes, either on facts relating to his particular case or of law in applying the rules governing seniority to those facts may be rectified. But once he has had that opportunity, it cannot possibly be said that he should have a further opportunity against even a final Seniority list. If he was to have that opportunity the list would not really be final but only provisional or preliminary. It will be obviously contradictory to hold it to be a final list and yet declare it subject to modifica tion on further objections. [829 E F] (3) The principle recognised in Shankarian 's Case, is confined to the facts and circumstances of that case. In order to establish the invalidity of the final List on some such grounds of invalidity, those grounds have to be shown to exist. It cannot possibly he said that if a final lists are prepared contrary to the rules applicable or is vitiated on some ground showing that a condition precedent to the finalisation of the lists is absent, it would still be inviolable. [830 A B] (4) The petitioner had ample opportunity to do that. He had ample opportunities to do so and the Central Government had also to give him those benefits.

The petitioners were granted Additional licences for import of rough diamonds and export of cut iron and steel. The import licence was renewed from time to time upto March 31, 1988. The petitioners were also granted additional licences on the basis of the Export Policy 1978 79. The respondents filed an application before the Customs & Excise Authorities under the Import & Export Policy, 1985 91 for grant of Additional Licences to Export Houses, claiming that the Export Houses had been granted Additional Licences in respect of import of raw materials and exports made in Appendices 3 to 218, 4 to 218 and 5 to 218. The said applications were rejected by the authorities on the ground that the petitioners had failed to establish that Export Houses who were issued Additional licences under the Imports & Exports Control Order 1978 were similarly situated. The petitioner filed writ petitions before this Court challenging the order of rejection contending that the respondents had violated the provisions of the Import and Export Policy 1979 79, and the restrictions imposed by the said orders were not only prohibited but also violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. This Court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) the Export House who were granted additional licence under the import policy for the period 1978 79 was similarly situated; (ii) the Additional Licences issued to Export houses, like the petitioners, would be valid for import only through Additional licences and (iii) the additional licences issued to the Export houses were similarly situate. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The licences issued in Appliedices 3 and 4 of the Imports and Exports 79 are valid for a period of twelve months and the said period has expired during the pendency of these writ petitions.[248C] 2.1 In order to successfully invoke the right guaranteed under Article 14, the petitioners have to establish their case before invoking the right of the respondents under the Export & Import Policy 197879.

The appellant assessee is a manufacturer of McCarcinston, falling under sub clause (i) of section 4(4)(d)(i) read with Explanation 2 to the Act. The appellant claimed that the manufactured goods were assessable to excise duty in respect of their product at the factory in packed condition and not in containers. The Assistant Collector of Central Excise held that the goods were delivered by a customer to a manufacturer on its own cost, that the assessee was not liable to pay the value of drums which were sold directly in tanks for the purpose of filling up the assessable value of such drums; that the appellant had not collected any amount in excess of the amount shown in the price list. The Appellate Collector of Customs affirmed this order. On further appeal by the Revenue, the Tribunal held that as the cost of packing was rental and hence should be included in the assessable values, the cost should be excluded in determining the assessable valuation. In reference, the High Court held that since the appellant did not spend any amount on the sale price for the purposes of excise duty, it could not be included under the assessablevalue. The Revenue appealed to this Court by special leave against the decision of the High court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i). the cost incurred by the appellant is a part of the assessable goods and must be included as a result of the process of manufacture; (ii) the cost in respect thereof should be deducted from the price charged by the assessee to its constituents; (iii) the value for the drums sold at the time of removal was not includible in the value under section 4 (4)(a); (iv) the packing charges were not includible and therefore, should be added to the assessable market value. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The cost of the packing is the oil which Excluded by the respondent assessee from the sale proceeds of the cylinders supplied by it. It has to be borne in mind that the measure of excise duties is price and not value. [994C] 2.1 The test to determine whether the cost is includable in the valuation of the goods for determining the "value" on the basis of the price paid or the raw material or component parts used in the manufacture or manufacture of the warehouse, is of a crucial importance. [89F] 1.2 In order to be goods, it was essential that as a consequence of the activitla tion, goods must come into existence. For all these reasons, the value has to include the cost price charged from the assessee. [90G] 2:3 The test is not generally to say that the articles supplied by the manufacturer are of a copartner or part of an incidental and incidental activity. It is necessary in order to determine the assessable nature of the supply. [91H; 92A] 1:4. In the instant case, the assessee had McDonaldon 's case, which was not applicable to the facts of the present case. The question whether the costs of packing were includible in a durable nature and should be taken into account in the assessment year in respect whereof the cost was incurred by it is only the cost which included the cost for the manufacture of excisable goods. [92B] 2(a) It is not necessary that the article must be sold at a particular point or point or returnable by the buyer to the assessee, and the question whether a notional amount representing the cost would be includible in its assessable value, if necessary, by addition to the sale prices charged by it to its constituent. [93C] (b) The test for determining "value ' in relation to any excisable goods is the same as that of the nature of payment or value withouttracted from the terms of the contract.

The appellant was an Accountant cum Headclerk in the Tamil Nadu Forest Training School at Vaigai Dam. He took charge of the office on 6.10.1975 and had been residing in a house opposite the training school. The appellant was charged with having committed food in the canteen for two days and being dissatisfied discontinued his practice before the notice was issued. The prosecution case was that the appellant had taken food in a canteen for three days and he was residing in another house opposite to the training School. The Trial Court accepted the prosecution evidence and convicted him under section 161 I.P.C. and section 336 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that there had been no independent evidence regarding the demand, the messenger who had contacted PW 1 at the behest of the appellant has not been examined, the solitary evidence of PW 1 is insufficient, the explanation offered by the appellant was probable and there was no conclusive evi dence to hold that the accused was guilty. On behalf of the respondent it was submitted that the evidence of PWs 1 and 2 is insufficient as the explanation tendered by the appel lant was probable, and there is no conclusive evidence to hold him guilty. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The conviction cannot be sustained. PW 3, the Principal has deposed in unequivocal terms that Ex. P2 memo had been issued on the basis of the complaint received from the appellant. The explanation offered for the absence of the accused is probable and reasonable. It must further be shown that the explanation was probable. [337C] 2. The evidence of the Principal shows that Ex PW 1, the principal has deposed that Ex P2 Memo had been executed on the same day. The fact that the conviction under section 5 (2) of Prevention of Corpo ration Act and section 5.(1)(a) of that Act are not attracted on the proved facts is also not impressive. [340D] 3. The High Court was right in holding that the prosecution had failed to prove the guilt conduct of the appe lant in view of the presumption arising under section 4(1) of Act which has not be en rebutted. The argument that clause (d) does not apply on the facts is rejected. [341E] Dhanvantrai Balwantrai Desai vs State of Maharashtra, AIR 1964 SC 575; C.I. Ernden vs State, AIR 1954 Saurashtra 12 1; and Dhanvantraj Balwantrai Balwantraj Desai vs state of Maharashtra ; , referred to.

The petitioner was an employee of a company which was in dire need of the flat in question. He retired from service on or about September 30, 1984. Prior to that date he addressed a letter requesting the Company to permit him to continue to live in the company 's premises during the period of his employment and that if he failed to do so he would be liable to pay higher compensation as per the company direction. The petitioner was informed by the Company that if the company failed to comply with the aforesaid request, it would be committing breach of section 630 of the Act. The Company filed a suit in the Court of Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Bombay for a declaration that he was a tenant of the disputed flat which is now pending. The City Civil & Sessions Judge held that the petitioner was wrongfully withholding the flat and directed issue of process. On appeal by the petitioner the High Court allowed the petition holding that section 630(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 makes it an offence where any officer or employee of the company wrongfully withholds possession of such property of the Company. The High Court also held that since the petitioner did not vacate the flat during the aforesaid period of service he committed an offence punishable under section 630. Allowing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The language of section 630(1)(a) of Bombay Rents Hotel and Rent Control Act is the only construction possible. It is quite evident that clauses (a) and (b) are separated by the word 'or ' and therefore are clearly disjunctive. The Court also observed that whenever the framers of the law in their wisdom thought it proper to bring within the mischief of the provisions of the said Act former officers or employees of a Company may withhold possession of any property of a limited company. It was further held that there was no warrant for the construction placed by the High court on the words 'any such property ' occurring in clause (b). [177E F] 1.2 The expression "any such" used in cl. (a), is wide enough to include former or past officer or employees if such officer oremployee either (a, wrongfully obtains possession of a property of another company during his employment, wrongfully withhold it after the termination of his employ. That appears to be one of the functions of cl. It would be rendered nugatory by projecting cl. The expression 'any other employee ' in cl.(b) is wider than the expression 'employee ' and, therefore, both clauses (b), (c) and sub section (1) are clearly conjunctive. [177F G] 2. In Amritlal Chum 's case, the Court held that clause (a)(i) by cls. (b)(ii) and cl.(c) of sub section(1), was in two parts. Sub section (I) by clauses (d) and Clause (b); sub section 2 makes it clear beneficent construction on the provision in furtherance of the object and purpose of the legislation which would suppress the mischief and advance the remedy.

The appellant was the founder of a Sansthan. The Sansthan was formed by the Maharaj who had been appointed as the manager of the Sansthan. In the year 1911, the Sansthan was given a lease of the property to be continued for ever by the British Government as the endowment property of the deity. The appellant 's father died in 1938 and his three sons were brought on record as legal representatives. The question for determination was whether the Sansthan is a private property or a public trust. The High Court held that the expression "the owner" in section 2(13) of the Act, includes a Malai 's son, and that the appellant was entitled to the property as a matter of right. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Sansthan being a private temple, its income is always liable to be assessed to tax under the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High court was not right in giving due importance to admission of the constituted attorney Ramkrishna Deshpande as the founder had no authority to do so. [528 B] (a) The appellant was a trustee for the Sansthan and was entitled as a religious endowment. The property was dedicated to the deity by the trustees. The temple was meant for the Darshan by the public. The object of the founder was to facilitate worship by the poor or Sansthan in regard to worship therein, the manner in which the property has been dealt with or managed by those in charge, the method in which it was used by the local people. [525 C D] (b) The High Courts were not right when the origin of the endowment is obscure and no direct oral evidence is available. The consciousness of the constituting attorney about the nature of the trust, which has been held out for more than a century as a public religious endowment, adds to the effect of the documentary evidence produced by the appellant in this case.

The appellant was a resident of Bombay. He was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 and 1951 52 under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876. The Income tax Officer issued a notice to him under section 14 of the Act calling upon him to show cause why he should not be apprehended and confined in his possession as if it were an arrear of land revenue. The appellant contended that the income tax authorities had no jurisdiction to recover the said amount from him. The Collector held that the appellant was liable to pay the tax under section 12(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the order of the Collector was not a valid one and that the Collector had no power to issue the said recovery. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the impugned law was based on a territorial classification having a reasonable nexus or correlation between the provisions of different laws which were applicable to each other, and (2) the imposition of tax under the Act was not violative of article 14 of 'the Constitution. HELD: (i) The contention must be negatived. (a) The expression "any person belonging to one State" in section 13(1)(b) of Bombay City Municipal Land Revenue Code, 1876 means that the collector is a territorial class and jurisdiction might be intended as or might have the effect of discrimination against a particular race or class where such race or classification is based on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group. The legislature has to devise for a particular purpose, namely, to provide for the detention of all defaulters for the same period in all cases in all States. [904 D E] (b) The object of article 13(i)(b), is to provide a speedy remedy for the recovery of public demand by putting pressure on the defaulter and it is not as if those provisions are set out in the Indian income tax Act in pari materia with the purpose of the Union. The object is that the law could not stand in the way of the enjoyment of fundamental rights. [0904 E F] (c) The word "law" in article 13 has to be given its widest connotation and it cannot be extended beyond what is necessary for the protection of the equal protection clause. It is a coercive process for recovery of arrears of land Revenue which are State demands. [1005 G H] (d) The distinction between the two statutes is that in the matter of payment of public demands of the States the people of Madras should be taken to subserve a purpose closely akin or similar to the purpose for which it has been devised. The former is a "law relating to various groups for the purpose" and the latter is levied under a single State law. [1105 G] (e) The two together constitute a territorial basis. It cannot be said that there was any territorial nexus or nexus between that basis of classification and the object sought to be achieved by the Indian Incometax Act. [1105 B C] (f) The argument that the tax is not a Union demand, therefore, must fail. [111 E F]. (g) The levy of tax on the assessee who was assessed under section 15 of the City of Bombay Municipal Land Reve nue Act, is not violative Of article 14 and therefore it was not open to the appellant to challenge the validity of the levy.

The respondent company was engaged in the business of shore crew. The respondent company had to establish a system of work and the shore ship was to be worked for 8 hours ' on any day in excess of the number of hours fixed by the Government. The workers were paid overtime wages at the minimum rate of wages in respect of which they had been paid. The company refused to accept the rates of work in view of the provisions of section 9A of the , and the Minimum Wages (Central) Rules, 1950. The Tribunal accepted the entire case put forward by the respondent company that the union was not able to establish that the existing system of working required any modification of the hours of work. The Union appealed to this Court. HELD : The workers had a 12 hour shift and there was no provision in the Act or the Rules corresponding to section 55 of the Factories Act for the fixation of minimum wages. The provisions of the and the Rules were subject to one more check which would be necessary if only those hours of duty were to be specified beforehand, and the workmen must pay overtime. [642 D] The working day of an adult can fix 48 hours of working day but by interval under section 13 is obviously meant interval of rest. It means a break in the work during which a workman, though present on duty, is not called upon to display either physical activity or sustained attention. But it is not a period of more inaction because there is no work for him. If it is the latter, it is counted as actual work period. [643 E] The provisions in section 9 A of the Act read with Rule 24 of the Rules are subject to two restrictions: (1) that the hours fixed for work in a six day week shall not spread over more than ten and a half hours in any day; and (2) that no worker shall be required or allowed to work in the factory for more than nine hours in a day. [641 F] The Act does not itself fix the hours for rest but only fixes the hours on each day in a week. It is wrong to contend that the period of 9 hours must always include intervals of rest and spread over ten days.

The appellant was the tenant of a shop in which he had let out on June 25, 1976. The accommodation was for the first time assessed for house tax by the Nagar Palika Ghaziabad with effect from October 1, 1976 and the suit was filed for eviction after termination of tenancy before the trial court and objection raised therein that as the shop and the basement were separately let out the tenancy could not be terminated by a single notice that would be invalid. The trial court dismissed the suit on the ground that since the shop was let out in June 1976, it was in that view of the matter that the appellant tenant will be entitled to protection under the Act. On appeal, the appellate court decreed the suit and held that the provisions of U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act 1972 would apply to these proceedings in view of section 39 of the Act and accordingly dismissed the plaintiff 's suit. The High Court set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and decreed the plaintiff suit. In appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) since the premises were let out for a first time under a licence which was for a short period from October l, 1976, the provisions in section 39 would be applicable to these premises; (ii) even if the matter is pending in this Court and 10 years have elapsed, the decree could not he passed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The rights of parties will be determined on the basis of the rights available to them on the date of the suit, but in Vineet Kumar vs Mangal Sain Wadhera, ; , this Court took the view that if during the pendency of the proceedings even of 10 years expired the protection will be available to the appellant but looking to the language of section 20 it appears that the contention of the appellants could not have been accepted. [166F G] 2.

The appellant was the tenant of a thika tenant. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for ejectment on the ground that he had been in arrears of rent from 1st October, 1949 to 31st December, 1949 and that the tenancy right therein had not been determined by the landlord as required by section 4(3) of the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act, 1949. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellant was entitled to eject the respondent under section 3 of the Act. On appeal the High Court held that the respondent was not liable to ejectment in view of the amendment of the definition of thika tenancy by Act II of 1953 which came into force on 1st November, 1949, and as such the respondent could not be regarded as a thikka tenant within the meaning of section 3(4) of that Act. The High Court further held that section 4 was prospective and did not apply to the case because the respondent had lost possession but any subsequent amendment of section 29 would not affect his rights under the Act, and that even if the appellant had lost the position in law as it stood before 1st December 1949, he could not claim protection of the provisions of the said Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the respondent 's right to evict the appellant under section 4 of the West Bengal General Clauses Act, 1899, had been barred by the amendment and (ii) the High Courts erred in holding that if the landlord wanted to eject a thka tenant after the Act had come into force, he was entitled not to eject him but only to eject his tenant. HELD: The appeal must be dismissed. (i)(a) The expression "any person who has already filed a claim for ejectment" in section 3 is not defined in the Act or in the Ordinance but as meaning a person who is not in possession and who has applied for relief under section 28 of the Indian Act, for the time being in force or in any contract. [182 B] (b) The word "successor" in the definition clause means a person claiming to get the protection of a right by making an application within three months of the commencement of the Ordinance. It is not necessary that there should be an application under section 5 after the expiry of the period of limitation as it finally emerged. [183 E] (c) The words "suitable" and "controlled" in sub section (1) of section 4 make it clear that a landlord who has filed a civil suit must show that the bar does not affect the case. [184 G] (d) Section 5 is prospective only. It could not apply where the decree or order for recovery of possession had been made before the date of commencement of Act. [185 B C] Mahadeolal Kanodia vs Administrator General of West Bengal, ; , followed. (e) The landlord who had filed a petition under section 14(1)(a), was entitled only to obtain the benefit of section 5 of the East Bengal General Clause Act, because he could have applied for the benefit thereof, and if he made an application for the same, he would not be entitled to any compensation. [186 G] Mahadolal vs AdministratorGeneral of WestBengal, ; and Mahadeholal Kanojodia vs Estate Officer, A.I.R. , referred to. (f) The proviso to section 4 is prospective and not retrospective. Section 5 being prospective only would apply to a case where the suit had been filed before the Act came into operation.

The State Government appointed a Pay Commission to consider the anomalies pointed out in the pay scales recommended by the U.P. Pay Commission. The recommendations were accepted and the High Court directed that the pay scale of Bench Secretaries be revised from Rs. 20000 to 30 per cent of the total cadre strength. The High Court also directed that all the posts of Bench Secretary should be upgraded and placed in the scale of Rs.500 1,000 as recommended by U. P. Pay Revision Commission. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the principle of equal pay for equal work had been violated; (ii) the High Courts completely ignored the fact that the posts were not of a higher nature and merely superiority; (iii) the recommendations of the U P. High Court were discriminatory and violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(g), 301 and 304 of the Constitution; and (iv) the pay structure recommended by State Government was contrary to the principles of equal Pay for equal Work. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of "equal pay for Equal work" is not expressly declared by this Court. [302G] 2.1 The High Courts are directed to consider whether the under privileged or weaker sections of the Department perform the same or similar work or duties. All India Services are to be the same, but quality may be different that cannot be translated into a mathematical formula. If it has a rational nexus with the object thereof. To hold otherwise, it would be detrimental to the interest of the service itself. [303H] 2:2 The principle is recognised by O. Chinnappa Reddy, J. in Randhir Singh vs Union of India and Others, ; , and Y.K. Mehta vs U.O.I., ; , referred to. 1.2 In matters of employment the Government of a socialist State must protect the weaker sections. It must be ensured that there is no exploitation of poor and ignorant. It is the duty of the State to see that the undered or weaker section of the society does not get their dues. Even if they have voluntarily accepted the employment on unequal terms, the State should normally accept it. The court should ordinarily accept it but should be determined by expert bodies like Pay Commission, pay scales and other emoluments. [304B C] 2(i) It is well established that the classification can be based on some qualities or characteristics of persons grouped together and not in others who are left out. Those qualities or charcteristics must, of course, have a reasonable relation to the object sought to be achieved. In service matters, merit or experience could be the proper basis for classification to promote efficiency in administration. He or she learns also by experience as much as by other means. It cannot be denied that the quality of work performed by persons of longer experience is superior than the work of newcomers. Even in Randhir Kaur 's case this principle has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. [305C D] 2.(ii) The classification made under the Rules, therefore, cannot be said to be violative of the right to have equal pay. After the argument was concluded in this appeal, counsel on both sides brought to our notice that the State Government had granted uniform pay scale for all posts of Senior Scale and Senior Scale Assistants with Superintendents of the Secretariat. The rules thus make a proper classification for the purpose of entitlement to higher pay scale. [306D E] 2 (iii). The High court has completely overlooked the criterion provided under the rules. The merit governs the grant of higher pay scales, cadre of Senior scale and that merit will be evaluated by a competent authority. The classification in this Bench 's pay scale is category wise.

The appellant company entered into an agreement with the respondent Company for the development of a municipal area known as the "Industrial Area" in consideration of its agreement dated June 24, 1973. Clause (d) of the agreement provided that the development scheme shall have to be framed and the State Government was to make provision for the regulation of the area tax and for the purpose of taxation and for matters connected therewith. The appellant company had entered into a contract with the appellant company for the construction of a building, a capital capital being owned by it. In accordance with the terms of the agreements, the respondent company agreed to pay property tax on the entry of goods into a factory. The agreement provided for the levy of development tax and the Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 was deemed to have come into force with effect from April 1, 1976. Section 127(d) provided that "the property tax shall not be leviable, inter alia, in respect of the following matters namely (a) building and lands owned by or vesting in the Union Government; (b) any land or building or both; (c) the buildings and lands or both. " The appellant Company was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913 with the object of carrying on business in the area of a municipality. In the year 1976, the State Legislature enacted the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961, which came into force from April l, 1976, by virtue of Entry 23 List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The respondent company was incorporated in the State of Madhya Pradesh and the appellant Company had been registered under the Madhya Bharat Municipal Corporation act, 1957. In respect of its property, the appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the agreement dated July 16, 1976 and the High court held that the property tax was not leviable on its property since it was owned wholly by the Government of India. The High Court also held that under section 127(a) of Act, 1973, the property taxes shall not exceed the prescribed percentage of the value of property. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the taxing authority must all the same apply its mind to the question whether it wants to bring to tax the land or buildings within their jurisdiction; and (ii) the provisions of the M.P. Municipalities Act were not in any way affected by the declaration contained in section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957, as amended by the Munici pal Amendment Act, 1964. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The State Legislature has enacted the Mica Mines Nationalisation Act,1973, for acquisition of coal mines with a view to reorganise and rehabilitate industrial areas. The Munic ipal is one of the matters which share the common need of the people in another. [14H; 15A] 2.1 The Mica Mining Corporation Act is an Act enacted by Parliament under Entry 23 of List II, Seventh Schedule, to provide for the constitution of a special area for the acquisition of mineral rights and for that purpose, the properties of the State or any authority within a State. The property tax is imposed by the State Legis lature on the Special Area Development Authority. [15D] 2(a). The M. P. Municipal Corporation is a 'State ' as defined in section 3(4) of The M .P. Municipal Act, 1922. The Act does not provide for any independent power of taxation or any machinery of its own for exercising the power of taxing authority. It rests content by pointing out that the M . P. Municipalities (Development & Regulation) Amendment Act 1957 has no application to the imposition of property tax. [16D] (b). The State legislature enacted the Coal Mines Nationalisation (Mines and Minerals) Act 1957, which was a part of the Act. The Parliament enacted the Mines & Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act. 1957.

The appellant was granted a lease for five years in respect of certain slate quarries within his estate for five year in succession. The appellant applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease and the Collector confirmed the lease. On appeal, the Collector held that the lease had been granted subsequent to July 1, 1945, and that as the lease was for a period exceeding one year, it was not enforceable against the Government. The question was whether the termination of the appellant 's lease by the order dated December 27, 1955, was bad as it did not give three months ' notice to the appellant or provide for any compensation as required by section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. Held, that the provisions of section 20 of the Act were applicable only to the termination and not to the Government 's right under the second proviso to section 20 (1). The words " such rights refer in the body of the section" in the third proviso meant a mere declaratory and the third Proviso was intended to be a self contained proviso. A. M. S.S. V.M. & Co. vs The State of Madras, ; , followed. The provisions of the Madras Estate (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, were applicable to the case as they applied only to rights created before the notified date but after July 1. 1945 for a further period exceeding two years. The effect of the second Proviso was that the Government must do something to avoid them. The third proviso was enacted to nullify the creation of rights in anticipation of the impending legislation and hence it was made unconditional.
